The non-gene entry 338090 is ranked last.

4255.Rationale: Infantile-onset syndromic neurodevelopmental picture: global developmental delay, growth delay, feeding difficulty, lethargy, spasticity, dystonia, seizures, abnormal speech, epicanthus, eyelid abnormality, abnormal facial shape, skeletal findings. 34367.Rationale: Infant-onset epilepsy, microcephaly, hypotonia/hypertonia, dystonia, pyramidal signs, migraine with aura, corpus callosum hypoplasia, ventriculomegaly and global developmental delay fit the ATP1A3 spectrum (developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, alternating hemiplegia, dystonia). I did not run a literature search.

13467.Rationale: Answered from recalled literature only; I did no searches. 30232.Rationale: Answered from recall, with no literature search or database lookup. The cause is ZEB2 haploinsufficiency, and ZEB2 carries a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 39, so it is the clear top candidate. 7455.Rationale: This is an inference from the phenotype list and the candidate gene list. I did not run a literature search or any tools. 2025.Rationale: No candidate fits the full phenotype well, so this ranking rests on partial matches and memory of the literature. I did not run a literature search or look up disease 440713. The picture is a multisystem neonatal or infantile disorder with cholestatic liver disease, steatorrhea, severe growth failure, flexion contractures, abnormal CNS myelination and subcortical atrophy. VPS35 is ranked first. It is a retromer component, and the retromer pathway is tied to VPS33B/VIPAS39 (arthrogryposis-renal dysfunction-cholestasis syndrome), which shares the cholestasis, contractures and growth failure. It is also the only candidate with a known late-onset disease (Parkinson disease 17), which would explain the 'elderly' onset label. KCTD7 (progressive myoclonic epilepsy with neurodegeneration) is next, because CNS myelination and atrophy abnormalities fit it best. SLC25A4 (mitochondrial disease) and TTN (myopathy and contractures) are lower. KCNQ5 (neurodevelopmental disorder) fits only weakly. MPL, PARPBP, PDE6H and SHPK have no plausible link to cholestasis or CNS myelination. MPL is also unlikely because anemia is absent.

9078.Rationale: Answered from recalled literature only. No searches were run. The picture is neonatal-onset arthrogryposis multiplex congenita with flexion contractures, neonatal asphyxia (respiratory failure at birth), progressive encephalopathy and craniofacial features (hypotelorism, shallow orbits, high forehead). This matches biallelic SLC6A9 (GlyT1) loss of function, which causes glycine encephalopathy with normal serum glycine (Kurolap et al. 2016). That condition presents with severe neonatal encephalopathy, hypotonia, arthrogryposis and respiratory failure. The rest of the neurodevelopmental genes (SRD5A3, SLC12A6, PEX6, SYNGAP1, NAA25, MBTPS2, SNCA for dyskinesia) fit only partially. 11111.Rationale: No literature or database lookup was done. The ranking comes from phenotype matching against what I remember of these genes, and the disease ID 440713 was not resolved. The phenotype set (abnormal CNS myelination, subcortical atrophy, short stature with severe postnatal growth retardation, hip and joint abnormalities, inguinal hernia, pain) best fits a lysosomal storage or neurodegenerative disorder such as HGSNAT-related MPS IIIC, which is also typically infant to childhood onset. BRCA1 is second because biallelic variants cause Fanconi anemia complementation group S, with severe growth retardation, short stature and congenital anomalies. RPS27A (Diamond-Blackfan anemia with congenital malformations and short stature) and SALL4 (congenital malformation syndromes) fit less well. SHPK, LZTR1 and MCF2L2 have no clear link to this phenotype, and LZTR1 is mainly a Noonan or schwannomatosis gene.

21929.Rationale: Ranking is a judgement call from memory. I did no literature search and could not identify Disease ID 440713. The phenotypes are a mixed, non-specific set: arthrogryposis, abnormal CNS myelination, hypopituitarism, macrocephaly with large fontanelles, and an infantile onset. TK2 (infantile mitochondrial myopathy with CNS involvement) and NEB (arthrogryposis from nemaline myopathy) fit best. ARSA (CNS myelination) and POMP (an infantile-onset disorder) come next. 25233.Rationale: Phenotypes are noisy and mixed. The strongest coherent signal is a mitochondrial fatty-acid beta-oxidation or hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase defect. Cholestasis, hepatitis, steatorrhea, severe postnatal growth retardation and short stature fit HADHA (LCHAD/trifunctional protein deficiency), which also carries a rare high-CADD splice/missense variant. HADH (SCHAD deficiency) is the next best fit, given the explicit 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase phenotype term and the hyperglycemia/insulin-regulation features, but no variant is listed for it. INSR is third, as it can explain growth retardation, macrocephaly and abnormal glucose handling, and it has a rare deleterious variant. The remaining genes have little link to the phenotype profile. NDUFAF2 and MT-TF are mitochondrial but point to a different phenotype (leukoencephalopathy or Leigh-like). I did not run a literature search, so this ranking rests on prior knowledge of these genes and the listed phenotypes.

28561.Rationale: Phenotype list is broad and noisy (arthrogryposis, large fontanelles, renal tubule, cholestasis, etc.), but the age of onset is elderly. GBE1 (adult polyglucosan body disease, adult or late onset with neurologic, bladder and systemic involvement) best fits the onset and multisystem picture. FN1 is next because it links to renal and skeletal dysplasia phenotypes (short stature, hip dysplasia, renal abnormality). It rests on prior knowledge only, and the disease ID 440713 was not looked up. The remaining candidates have no clear link to the phenotypes or onset.

31236.Rationale: Prioritised from background knowledge of the literature; I ran no searches. The core picture is infantile-onset arthrogryposis and flexion contractures, neck muscle weakness, breech presentation and neonatal asphyxia (both consistent with fetal hypokinesia), short stature, and keloids, together with rimmed vacuoles on muscle biopsy. Keloid formation plus early contractures is a hallmark of collagen VI-related myopathy (Bethlem/Ullrich spectrum), which matches COL6A3 best. COL6A3 also has the highest CADD among the myopathy genes (45). GMPPB (dystroglycanopathy with congenital onset), DYSF, and CAV3 (limb-girdle/rippling-muscle phenotypes, with hypertriglyceridemia and rimmed vacuoles reported in some muscle disorders) are next. HDAC8 (Cornelia de Lange-like, X-linked, short stature, abnormal facies) is a plausible secondary contributor for the dysmorphic features. SAR1B (chylomicron retention disease) would fit the steatorrhea, but the absence of diarrhea and hypocholesterolemia argues against it. The remaining genes have little or no link to this phenotype.

29957.Rationale: No literature or database lookup was done; this ranking comes from recall of gene-phenotype associations. The core features are prenatal-onset: arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, flexion contractures, breech presentation and neonatal respiratory distress. Together they suggest a congenital neuromuscular disorder. TRIP4 (and ASCC1) is linked to prenatal-onset spinal muscular atrophy with arthrogryposis, respiratory failure and sometimes bone fractures, and the candidate has a high-CADD splice/missense variant. SMN1 causes type 0/1 SMA with arthrogryposis and respiratory distress. It has no listed variant, which fits a deletion that the variant calls may not capture. FKTN causes dystroglycanopathy with contractures, macrocephaly and developmental delay and has a high-CADD variant. DHX38, GLI3 and SMN2 are lower-probability candidates. The other genes (CIDEA, P2RX7, SHPK, CHAF1B, ZAP70, NT5C2, DCAF17) have no good fit to the main phenotype and are placed last. The cholestasis and renal tubular features resemble ARC syndrome (VPS33B/VIPAR), but neither gene is among the candidates.

34884.Rationale: Answered from memory without a literature search, and none of the candidates clearly fits the full phenotype. The presentation combines CNS hypomyelination and subcortical atrophy with neonatal-onset liver disease (cholestasis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, fat malabsorption), arthrogryposis and severe growth retardation. The aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes fit best. RARS1 (listed as RARS11) causes hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, which matches the abnormal CNS myelination and atrophy. MARS2 is a mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase gene with CNS involvement, but its known phenotype (spastic ataxia) lacks the liver features. PCSK1 is weakly relevant through malabsorption and growth failure. The remaining genes (DYSF, CEP55, WDR48, ATN1, PRKCG, SHPK, ITGA8, ESR2, KCNIP3) have no clear link to this combination of hepatic, CNS and joint findings.

39737.Rationale: Disease ID 440713 could not be resolved to a disease from memory, and I did no literature or database lookup, so these scores rest on phenotype matching alone. They also involve liver disease (cirrhosis), brain atrophy, short stature, joint contractures and metabolic or GI abnormalities, which fit this profile. 34123.Rationale: No literature or web searches were run, so this ranking comes from prior knowledge and the phenotype profile. They are ranked low.

22551.Rationale: Phenotype set is dominated by neurological and musculoskeletal features: arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, flexion contractures, hip dysplasia, breech presentation (reduced fetal movement), ventriculomegaly and hydrocephalus, Chiari malformation, abnormal CNS myelination, short stature. DYNC1H1 (dynein heavy chain) fits best: dominant-negative missense variants cause neurodevelopmental disorders with cortical malformation, abnormal myelination, ventriculomegaly and arthrogryposis, and it carries a very high CADD of 62. TNXB is second: connective-tissue disorders with joint contractures, hip dysplasia, diastasis recti and Chiari-type findings. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of the genes; I did not search the literature.

25011.Rationale: This ranking comes from prior knowledge. I did not run a literature search. Short stature, small testes and toe macrodactyly fit a CDKN1C growth and gonadal disorder (IMAGe, Beckwith-Wiedemann or Silver-Russell spectrum). The variant is also a rare, high-CADD splice/missense change. RMRP (cartilage-hair hypoplasia spectrum) explains short stature, but the variant is non-coding and less specific. 40787.Rationale: No literature or web search was run. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of the genes. The phenotype set (arthrogryposis, cholestasis, portal hypertension, renal tubular abnormality, growth retardation, steatorrhea) resembles ARC syndrome (VPS33B/VIPAS39), but neither gene is in the candidate list. FAT4 (Van Maldergem/Hennekam, craniofacial and renal features) and ABCC6 (xanthelasma-like skin and connective tissue disease) follow. GRHL3 and STXBP1 come next. The rest have weaker phenotype links.

16225.Rationale: Infantile onset with nystagmus, abnormal involuntary eye movements, hypometric saccades, strabismus, generalized hypotonia, global developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, abnormal reflexes and abnormal speech suggests a neurodevelopmental or hypomyelinating disorder. SLC5A7 (presynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome / neuromuscular disorder; the AChR antibody positivity could point toward a neuromuscular junction disorder) is a strong second, with a rare splice/missense variant. CFAP410 (ciliopathy/retinal) is a weaker fit for the eye findings. CUBN, LZTS1 and the remaining genes have no clear link to this phenotype. This ranking is from recalled literature, and I did not run any literature or database search.

36639.Rationale: Phenotype is a childhood-onset neurodevelopmental picture with cognitive impairment, seizures, hypotonia, dysarthria, scoliosis, strabismus and abnormal saccadic or paroxysmal eye movements, which suggests a cerebellar-type disorder. This best fits RORA (intellectual developmental disorder with or without epilepsy or cerebellar ataxia), where the candidate variant is rare, splice/missense and has a high CADD of 36. KANSL1 (Koolen-de Vries: hypotonia, seizures, ID, strabismus) is next. ZC4H2, RPS6KA3 and HCN4 are lower. The absent terms (large hands, joint contractures, mild ID, myopathy) argue against Coffin-Lowry (RPS6KA3) and ZC4H2-related arthrogryposis. Genes with no variants, or with no neurological link to the phenotype, are placed last. I did not do a literature search; this ranking is from prior knowledge of the gene-phenotype associations.

865.Rationale: No literature or database lookup was performed, so this ranking rests on phenotype-to-gene matching from memory. 18484.Rationale: No literature or web search was run. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of the genes and the phenotype profile. ADSL and SOX5 explain seizure and hypotonia only partly, since intellectual disability and developmental delay are marked absent. The remaining genes have little overlap with this phenotype set.

19111.Rationale: No literature search was run, so this ranking is from phenotype matching only. 28440.Rationale: This ranking comes from the supplied phenotypes and variant annotations plus recalled knowledge. I ran no literature search and did not classify variants. 21351.Rationale: This is an inference from recalled knowledge. I did not run a literature search or any tool lookups. 36187.Rationale: Ranked from the phenotype list and general knowledge of these genes. I did not run a literature or database search, and I could not identify what Disease ID 512260 refers to. 30361.Rationale: Infantile-onset cerebellar syndrome (ataxia, dyssynergia, vermis and cerebellar atrophy, nystagmus, dysarthria, delayed motor development, seizures) with spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski sign explicitly absent. 32230.Rationale: Disease ID 1997 is likely blepharocheilodontic syndrome (CDH1), but I did not look this ID up. This is a judgement from memory, not a literature review. 26709.Rationale: Based on knowledge of the phenotype pattern only, with no literature search done. 12789.Rationale: Based on prior knowledge only; I did not run a literature search or open web search. 19017.Rationale: Ranking is from recalled literature only; I ran no searches. NCOR1 (autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability) and ASH2L (neurodevelopmental disorder) follow as plausible neurodevelopmental genes. AIFM1 (X-linked neuropathy/ID) and ASAH1 (spinal muscular atrophy with myoclonic epilepsy) are plausible but fit less well. STAT1 and SOS1 are immune and RASopathy genes and fit poorly. SPTA1 (erythrocyte morphology was absent), RMDN3 and ZFR have little link to this phenotype.

26565.Rationale: This is a judgement from the phenotype list and general knowledge of the genes. I did not run a literature search and could not identify disease 476126. The core picture is neurodevelopmental: global developmental delay, poor speech, autistic and aggressive behavior, seizures, and tremor. Skeletal and craniofacial features accompany it: scoliosis, pectus excavatum, pes planus, high palate, dental crowding with eruption failure, long philtrum, short nose, feeding difficulty and failure to thrive. NFIX (Malan and Marshall-Smith spectrum) fits this combination best. TRIO (autosomal dominant intellectual disability with behavioral problems and dysmorphism) is second. The mitochondrial findings (abnormal muscle mitochondria, ophthalmoplegia, EMG abnormality, early death) point to PDPR and HADHA. The other candidates (HDAC2, SLC33A1, KIF22, INVS, MESP2, and so on) match few of the features. AGT, HADH, CYP21A2, AGXT, RSPH3 and similar genes belong to unrelated phenotypes, and several are explicitly excluded by the absent phenotypes (adrenal insufficiency, immotile cilia, skeletal dysplasia, vertebral segmentation defect).

25430.Rationale: The phenotype is a congenital myopathy: generalized hypotonia, limb and neck weakness, and decreased fetal movement. Biopsy shows minicores, centrally nucleated fibers and increased fiber size variability, with myopathic EMG. Scoliosis, high palate, recurrent respiratory infections and motor delay fit the same picture. This pattern, especially minicore myopathy with central nuclei, is classic for RYR1-related myopathy (multiminicore disease / centronuclear myopathy), and RYR1 carries a rare, high-CADD splice/missense variant. TRIP4 (ASC-1 complex) is the next most plausible candidate, since it causes recessive congenital myopathy and muscular dystrophy-like disease with hypotonia and respiratory involvement. The renal, cardiac, ovarian and brain findings are not explained by RYR1, but no other candidate explains the muscle phenotype. I made this call from prior knowledge of these genes and did not search the literature for this case. ABCC8 and TRIM28 are only weak possibilities. The remaining genes have no clear link to a congenital myopathy.

30380.Rationale: Phenotype is a slowly progressive myopathy with centrally nucleated fibers, myopathic EMG, neck weakness, respiratory insufficiency, scoliosis, high palate, joint laxity, follicular hyperkeratosis, dry skin and skin rash. This was ranked from recalled literature, not a fresh literature search. TRIP4 (ASC-1 complex) deficiency causes a congenital muscular dystrophy/myopathy with respiratory insufficiency, scoliosis, joint laxity and hyperkeratosis or ichthyosis-like skin changes, which matches best. TRAPPC11 (LGMD R18) comes next as a myopathy with scoliosis and high palate. HACD1 gives a centronuclear-like congenital myopathy. DYSF and COL7A1 are weaker fits, and the remaining candidates are unrelated.

24624.Rationale: Answered from recalled knowledge of the literature; no search or database lookup was run, and I did not confirm that Disease ID 442835 is a Cockayne syndrome entry. The phenotype set fits Cockayne syndrome / UV-sensitive nucleotide-excision-repair disease: early-onset encephalopathy, microcephaly, failure to thrive with cachexia, abnormal myelination, optic atrophy, nystagmus, ataxia, tremor, hypotonia, reduced reflexes, intellectual disability and speech delay, plus skin findings, infertility and frontal balding. ERCC6 (CSB) is the classic Cockayne syndrome gene. It also carries a rare splice/missense candidate variant with the highest CADD score in the list (44). AIFM1 is the next best fit. Its X-linked disease spectrum includes infantile encephalopathy, hypomyelination, ataxia, optic atrophy and neuropathy. The remaining candidates (PRKAR1A, SLC13A5, FGFR2, CBS, NKX2-1 and others) match poorly or are excluded by the negative phenotypes. For example, the absent amino acid metabolism abnormality, ectopia lentis, arachnodactyly and tall stature argue against CBS/Marfan-type or homocystinuria-type disease. Other genes were ranked on weaker partial overlap, such as PRKAR1A for skin/melanoma-type features and SLC13A5 for infantile encephalopathy.

11204.Rationale: This ranking comes from recalled knowledge of the literature. I did not run any searches or verify anything against sources. The picture is an infantile-onset severe neurodevelopmental disorder: microcephaly, intellectual disability, seizures, cerebral visual impairment, sensorineural hearing loss, corpus callosum hypoplasia, cerebellar atrophy, oromotor apraxia, and joint contractures with ankylosis. The pertinent negatives (no ataxia, nystagmus, tremor, myokymia, dysarthria or hyperparathyroidism) argue against KCNA1, FGF14 and CDC73. VPS11-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy (HLD12) fits best: microcephaly, severe developmental delay, seizures, cortical visual impairment, thin corpus callosum, cerebellar atrophy and hearing loss. BCAP31 (deafness, dystonia and cerebral hypomyelination syndrome) fits next on SNHL, seizures, microcephaly and contractures. DNM1L encephalopathy is a plausible third, though optic atrophy is recorded as absent. DDRGK1 and SIRT1 are weaker, with some neurodevelopmental or skeletal overlap. The remaining genes have no good phenotypic match: ST14 and KRT6B are skin disorders, ABCC2 causes Dubin-Johnson syndrome, and F11 is a coagulation gene with no variant listed. The protein S and hypochromic anemia findings are likely incidental.

21226.Rationale: The phenotype is an infantile-onset severe neurodevelopmental encephalopathy: microcephaly, global developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, central hypotonia, optic atrophy, growth delay, contractures, cerebellar atrophy and abnormal speech. This matches DNM1L-related encephalopathy due to defective mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission, which is also linked to optic atrophy. The DNM1L variant is a splice/missense change with CADD 41 and is rare. This is from recalled literature, not a fresh search. MED12 (X-linked ID syndromes with hypotonia) is a plausible second choice. MGME1 and OPA1 are mitochondrial genes that fit partly, but OPA1 has no observed variant and the negative findings (no PEO, no visual impairment, no white matter abnormality) argue against them. VPS11 is a leukodystrophy gene, and white matter morphology is absent here. The other genes (CPT2, DNMT1, ANK3, COL9A3, BLK, PRNP, NOTCH3, NOTCH4) fit the phenotype poorly.

30578.Rationale: Answer is from recalled literature, not a live search. The phenotype fits TRAPPC11-related disease best: infantile-onset global developmental delay, intellectual disability, absent speech, seizures, central hypotonia, microcephaly, cerebellar atrophy, white matter abnormality, elevated CK, hypothyroidism, diabetes, hepatic involvement and joint contractures. TRAPPC11 also carries the highest CADD score (40) in the list. VPS11 is second because it causes a hypomyelinating leukoencephalopathy with ID, seizures, hypotonia, microcephaly and visual impairment. DDRGK1 ranks third on its multisystem and ER-related disease associations. KIF1C and MGME1 are down-weighted because ataxia and progressive external ophthalmoplegia are listed as absent. GYG1 is unlikely because it causes a muscle-restricted glycogen storage disease and muscle weakness is absent. The remaining genes have no known link to this syndrome.

21899.Rationale: The positive phenotypes (adult-onset dementia, memory and cognitive impairment, senile plaques, frontotemporal and diffuse cerebral atrophy, apathy, behavioral change) fit late-onset Alzheimer disease. The negative phenotypes (spastic paraplegia, lipid and biliary findings) look unrelated to this disease and appear to come from other diseases. CLU (clusterin) is an established Alzheimer disease GWAS locus tied to amyloid plaque biology, and it carries a rare candidate variant here, so I rank it first. Next are genes with neurodegeneration or dementia links: HSD17B10 (HSD10 mitochondrial disease, which binds amyloid-beta), SGSH (Sanfilippo A, with dementia and behavioral change), TRPM2 (neurodegeneration, dementia and oxidative stress), GABRA1, DDX3X, COG4, and MICOS13 (mitochondrial). The remaining genes (MUC16, RLBP1, MLLT11, PSTPIP1, SMARCA4, MYCN, PRKAR1B, KLHL1, RMDN2, LIPC, SC5D, COL11A2, ANAPC2, APC2, 100049707) have no clear link to this phenotype. This ranking rests on prior knowledge of the literature; I did not run any searches or variant classification.

25360.Rationale: Adult-onset behavioral/frontotemporal-type dementia (inappropriate behavior, apathy, short attention span, mental deterioration, frontotemporal atrophy, abnormal neuron morphology) with absence of motor neuron or spastic signs. This fits the recently described PRKAR1B-related neurodegenerative dementia (recurrent missense variants in the PKA regulatory subunit RIbeta, with neuronal protein aggregation and dementia). I am recalling this from the literature and did not search to confirm it. The other candidates are weaker. HSD17B10 and NDUFB10 are mitochondrial/neurometabolic genes. SLC25A32 and RTN1 have only loose neurological links. The rest have no plausible link to this phenotype. The cardiac, renal, pulmonary and vascular phenotypes look like noise.

2788.Rationale: No literature search was run. This ranking comes from phenotype-to-gene matching alone and is low confidence, because no candidate is a classic aortic aneurysm or connective-tissue gene such as COL3A1 or FBN1. LMX1B (nail-patella spectrum) fits hematuria, scoliosis, pectus, joint dislocation and pain, and it carries a rare, high-CADD splice/missense variant. CACNA1C (Timothy-type syndromes) fits PDA, valve and cardiac anomalies, and it also carries a variant. ADA2 (DADA2) fits vasculopathy and aneurysm, bleeding, hematuria and pituitary involvement, but it has no observed variant. NOD2 (Blau syndrome) is less likely because skin rash and keratitis are absent. The remaining genes fit the phenotype poorly: they are neuropathy, retinal, mitochondrial, neurodevelopmental or myopathy genes, and the phenotype list contains none of those features.

19269.Rationale: The core phenotype is childhood-onset complex spastic paraplegia with spastic paraparetic gait, upper motor neuron weakness, dystonia, hyperkinetic movements, seizures, poor head control and feeding difficulties. This best fits FA2H-related disease (SPG35 / fatty acid hydroxylase-associated neurodegeneration), which is autosomal recessive and causes spastic paraplegia, dystonia, seizures and cognitive and behavioral problems. FA2H carries a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 35. FARS2 is second: it causes mitochondrial disease with seizures and, in some patients, a spastic paraplegia phenotype (SPG77). CACNA2D1 is a weaker candidate, with epilepsy and neurodevelopmental associations. The remaining genes (LPAR2, FLT4, OBSL1, IL2RG, NOG, RECQL4) are linked to unrelated phenotypes (hearing loss, lymphedema, 3-M syndrome, SCID, symphalangism, Rothmund-Thomson syndrome) and do not explain the neurological picture. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of these genes and was not checked against the literature or any database.

34893.Rationale: Infantile onset with developmental regression, dystonia, myoclonus, axial hypotonia, lower limb spasticity, mitochondrial-type muscle abnormality and laryngospasm suggests a mitochondrial or hereditary spastic paraplegia/dystonia disorder. FARS2 (mitochondrial phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase; SPG77 and infantile mitochondrial encephalopathy) has a rare deleterious splice/missense variant and fits best. CYP2U1 (SPG56, spastic paraplegia with dystonia) is next. ATAD3A (hypotonia, mitochondrial dysfunction, dystonia) and GCDH (dystonia, but dyskinesia is absent) follow. ST3GAL5 (infantile-onset neurodevelopmental disorder) is less consistent because seizures are absent. The remaining genes have no clear link to this neurological and mitochondrial phenotype. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of these genes; I did not run a literature search.

17220.Rationale: The core phenotype is intellectual disability, neurodevelopmental delay, poor speech, feeding difficulty, seizures, VSD, cryptorchidism and hypospadias, inner ear dysfunction, and mild facial dysmorphism (eyebrow, anteverted nares). This overlaps most with CHARGE-like and urogenital-cardiac syndromes. CHD7 carries a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 36. It fits ear, heart and genital anomalies with intellectual disability and seizures. UBA2 carries a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 37. Its haploinsufficiency syndrome has hypospadias, cryptorchidism, cardiac defects and neurodevelopmental delay. ARX fits X-linked intellectual disability, seizures and genital anomalies, but it has no observed variant and corpus callosum agenesis is absent. YWHAZ and PSMD10 are neurodevelopmental candidates with rare damaging variants, but they match the genital and cardiac features less well. PHB2 and MT-ND2 relate to the mitochondrial finding, but the phenotype is not typical of either. The remaining genes (KCNJ11, ABCA4, FRAS1, CEP85L, CTSF, VPS51, RNASE1, RAC1) do not match the main features. FRAS1 has some urogenital relevance but is recessive, and RAC1 is a neurodevelopmental gene but has no observed variant.

15613.Rationale: Answered from recalled knowledge only; I did not search the literature or run any tools, and I could not identify what disease ID 500159 refers to. The phenotype is a neurodevelopmental syndrome with hypotonia, global and motor delay, poor speech, stereotypies, facial dysmorphism (maxillary hypoplasia, plagiocephaly), PDA, scoliosis, growth delay and keloids. RAC1 (dominant intellectual disability, MRD48) best fits this pattern of hypotonia, developmental delay and dysmorphism, so I ranked it first. The absent macrocephaly argues against it only partly, because RAC1 phenotypes vary in head size. The absent myopathy, myotonia, reflex loss and pectus excavatum argue against FHL1. The absent eye-movement abnormalities, strabismus and oculomotor palsy argue against MAFB (Duane retraction syndrome). Several other genes carry rare high-CADD splice/missense variants but have no clear link to this phenotype (POLG, WRN, ABCA7, APOE, CFH, CASQ2, SLC25A37, RNASE1, AHNAK2). TBX1 (cardiac and craniofacial features), GLI3 (polydactyly absent, so a poor fit) and FGFR3 (scoliosis, craniofacial) are only partial matches. NCOA6 is a speculative second choice: it has a variant, and a coactivator-related syndrome with keloids and a CNS tumour is conceivable, but I have no evidence for it.

37526.Rationale: Answered from recalled literature only; no searches or tools were run. The core picture is infantile-onset intellectual disability with global developmental delay, microcephaly, seizures, ventriculomegaly, VSD/PDA, feeding difficulties and facial dysmorphism. This fits RAC1-related autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder (MRD48), which features microcephaly (or macrocephaly), structural brain anomalies, seizures and congenital heart defects. RAC1 has no variant listed here, but the neurodevelopmental phenotype still matches best. The negative findings (no Krebs-cycle abnormality, no raised CSF lactate, no ataxia) argue against a primary mitochondrial cause, so MT-ND1 is ranked lower despite its missense variant. HSD17B10 (HSD10 disease) overlaps on ID, seizures, cardiac involvement and hearing loss, but it is X-linked and the acylglycine profile is normal, so it ranks second. Other genes (ABCC8 for diabetes, SPECC1L and TP63 for craniofacial features, NKX2-1, MRE11, TINF2, RMRP and the rest) explain only isolated features or are unrelated, so they get low scores. The many other phenotypes in the list (coronary calcification, MI, venous thrombosis, autoimmune antibodies, spinal cord compression) look like unrelated noise.

17505.Rationale: The core phenotype is male infertility with oligozoospermia and reduced sperm motility, which fits the male infertility gene group. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge only; I did not run a literature search or check the disease ID. TEX11 (X-linked meiotic gene) is a known cause of spermatogenic failure, with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia. SUN5 causes acephalic spermatozoa with reduced motility and is the next best fit. EGR3 is a weak candidate: Egr3-knockout mice show sensory ataxia and behavioral abnormalities, which could explain the neurological terms, but not the sperm findings. CX3CL1, CASR and GALNS have no clear link to male infertility, so they are ranked last.

21435.Rationale: Based on prior knowledge only; I did not run a literature search. The core phenotype is isolated adult male infertility with abnormal sperm motility, and oligozoospermia is explicitly absent. SUN5 is the only candidate with an established sperm-specific role. It is a known cause of male infertility through sperm head-tail coupling defects, and it carries a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 35. Acephalic spermatozoa is listed as absent, which weakens the fit, but SUN5 variants can produce a spectrum of sperm morphology and motility defects. ALMS1 is second because Alstrom syndrome involves obesity (overweight is present) and male hypogonadism or infertility, and its variant has the highest CADD (62). PNPLA6 and DHH come next for their links to hypogonadism and gonadal or testis dysfunction. The remaining genes have no clear link to sperm motility or male infertility and are ranked low. RPGRIP1 is a ciliopathy gene, so it ranks slightly higher among them. MBTPS2, CDC45, GFAP, DNASE1L3 (cellulitis and immune links) and the others are largely unrelated.

9419.Rationale: Answer from memory only; no literature search was run, so confidence is low. The phenotype combines dental and oral features (gingival fibromatosis, narrow palate, delayed tooth eruption, enamel defects), ectodermal features (hyperkeratosis, brittle hair), sensorineural hearing loss and some systemic features. The absent terms (ichthyosis, albinism or hypopigmentation, bleeding, immunodeficiency, optic atrophy, radioulnar synostosis) look like exclusions for the other candidates. That makes HPS1, AP3B1 and BLOC1S6 (Hermansky-Pudlak), HOXA11, OPA1 and CLDN1 less likely. EVC2 fits best because it causes dental and enamel anomalies, a narrow palate, delayed eruption and gingival and oral changes, with the ectodermal involvement seen in Ellis-van Creveld and Weyers syndromes. MED12 is a plausible X-linked syndromic option, and TRAF6 and CLDN1 are weaker ectodermal or epithelial candidates. The remaining genes have no clear link to this phenotype.

7677.Rationale: This is a ranking from recall only. I did no literature search or database lookup, so the order is a judgement call. The phenotype combines infantile-onset neurodevelopmental disease (intellectual disability, seizures, failure to thrive, optic nerve hypoplasia) with diabetes, conductive hearing loss, osteolysis, joint and dental anomalies, and low riboflavin. PTPN23 (neurodevelopmental disorder with structural brain anomalies and seizures, with optic nerve involvement) fits the neuro-ophthalmic core best. MT-ATP6 fits a multisystem mitochondrial picture (diabetes, seizures, hearing loss, intellectual disability, low riboflavin) and carries a damaging missense variant (PP2=1.0). FLNB and RECQL4 account for some of the skeletal, joint, dental and telangiectasia features, but several of their expected features are listed as absent (joint dislocations, rash, nail changes, growth delay). PTPN11, KCNMA1 (seizures, intellectual disability) and DPM3 are weaker neurodevelopmental fits. KIT, KLHL3, EPAS1, BLOC1S3, HIVEP1 and the remaining genes match the listed absent phenotypes (mastocytosis, hyperkalemia and hypertension, pheochromocytoma, hypopigmentation, immunodeficiency) or lack a link to the positive features, so they are ranked low.

17990.Rationale: Phenotype set (infant onset, intellectual disability, seizures, failure to thrive, delayed tooth eruption, hirsutism, ocular anterior-segment anomaly, hearing impairment, osteolysis, narrow palate) best fits Ramon-type syndrome / ELMO2-related disorder (ELMO2 also linked to osteolysis and intraosseous vascular anomalies). This is from recall of the literature, not a fresh search. Absent gingival fibromatosis argues somewhat against it. DCAF17 (Woodhouse-Sakati: diabetes, hearing loss, ID, hypogonadism) and SMARCA4 (Coffin-Siris: ID, hirsutism, delayed development) are the next best fits. HBA1/HBA2 explain hydrops fetalis, but only partially. LMF1 is disfavored because hypertriglyceridemia and chylomicronemia are absent. Other genes have weak or partial overlap.

12276.Rationale: Answered from phenotype matching only; no literature or web search was run. FLNA fits best. Megaduodenum (intestinal pseudo-obstruction), hydrocephalus, hearing impairment, hypertelorism, cryptorchidism in a male, short stature, delayed skeletal maturation and a facial gestalt of hypertelorism, deep philtrum and macrotia match the FLNA spectrum (otopalatodigital/frontometaphyseal dysplasia, periventricular heterotopia with hydrocephalus, X-linked intestinal pseudo-obstruction). Against this, abnormal palate and brachydactyly are listed as absent. PPP1CB is second because the webbed neck, hypertelorism, cryptorchidism, short stature, intellectual disability and low-set ears fit a Noonan-like syndrome. Pulmonic stenosis, sparse hair and lymphadenopathy are listed as absent, which lowers that fit. NSD1 (Sotos) is unlikely because tall stature and large-for-gestational-age are absent. CTNNB1 and PAX2 each explain only a few features (intellectual disability, hearing or renal findings). The remaining genes are poor fits for this phenotype set.

7628.Rationale: The picture is an infantile multisystem disorder: hepatosplenomegaly with reduced liver function, low copper (low ceruloplasmin, a typical sign of a congenital disorder of glycosylation), global developmental delay, spasticity, cerebral atrophy, secondary microcephaly, corpus callosum hypoplasia and a small pituitary. This fits a Golgi glycosylation defect best. COG4 (COG4-CDG, CDG-IIj) and COG2 are the conserved oligomeric Golgi complex genes in the list. COG4 carries a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 37, so it ranks first. COG2 is second as the other COG subunit. The other candidates have rare variants but their known phenotypes do not match. Examples are retinal genes (EYS, ABCA4, CFH), cardiac (TNNT2) and the X-linked RPS6KA3. TUBB4A, MTTP and FH have some neurological or hepatic overlap but are weaker fits. I worked from prior knowledge and did not run a literature search.

42262.Rationale: Based on my own knowledge of these genes. I did not do a literature search or open web search. Key discriminating features are seizures, intellectual disability, hypotonia, irritability, growth delay, sensorimotor neuropathy, upper motor neuron signs and cystathioninuria. PLPBP (vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy) fits seizures, hypotonia, irritability, ID and growth delay, and cystathioninuria is a recognized biochemical finding in it, so it is ranked first. CLP1 (pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 10) fits seizures, ID, hypotonia, poor head control, sensorimotor neuropathy, spasticity and hyperreflexia. No variant is listed for CLP1, which lowers confidence. FA2H and REEP2 (spastic paraplegia) fit the upper motor neuron signs and hyperreflexia. SCN1A fits seizures but not the neuropathy or cystathioninuria. SLC26A4-AS1 is only a weak match through enlarged vestibular aqueduct. The remaining genes have no clear phenotype match.

14900.Rationale: Ranked from memory only; I did no literature search and could not identify Disease ID 464440. The dominant features are adult-onset dystonia (oromandibular, laryngeal, limb), bradykinesia and tremor. That pattern best fits ATP13A2 (Kufor-Rakeb / PARK9 dystonia-parkinsonism), which also has a rare, deleterious-looking splice/missense variant (CADD 36). PITX3 explains the cataract and ocular anterior-segment findings. APOC3 is plausible for the lipid and atherosclerosis features, but hyperlipidemia is listed as absent. MT-ATP6 is a possible cause of movement disorder and dystonia. HDAC8 has the highest CADD (62) but fits the phenotype poorly. The remaining genes have little phenotypic connection to the case.

18781.Rationale: The main positive phenotypes are adult-onset focal dystonia and action tremor. Limb dystonia is marked absent, which fits an isolated focal or cranio-cervical dystonia. COL6A3 (DYT27, recessive dystonia with cervical, cranial and segmental involvement) is the best fit. It also carries a high-CADD rare splice/missense variant. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge, not a literature search, and I did not confirm what Orphanet disease 464440 is. The other phenotypes (hyperkalemia, thrombocytopenia, laryngeal web and so on) look like noise and do not point to one gene. TBX19 (ACTH deficiency), FANCD2 (leukemia/Fanconi), RPS28 (Diamond-Blackfan anemia) and the ciliopathy genes CSPP1 and B9D1 do not match the focal dystonia picture. TBX19 and FANCD2 are further disfavoured because ACTH deficiency, low cortisol, neonatal hypoglycemia and acute leukemia are marked absent. KCNH1, KCNAB2, FGF13, KCNK2, DST and WDR1 are neurological or ion-channel genes with weaker links, so I ranked them as secondary.

8002.Rationale: Answered from recall of the literature, with no searches run, and I could not confirm what Disease 399081 is. The core picture is adolescent-onset progressive distal weakness with loss of ambulation, absent Achilles reflex, axonal neuropathy and myopathic EMG. That fits a neuromuscular disease with both nerve and muscle involvement. DNM2 causes dominant intermediate CMT type B and axonal CMT2M, and the same gene causes centronuclear myopathy. The absent centrally nucleated fibers, normal CK and no floppy infant argue against the centronuclear myopathy form, but not against the neuropathy form. KLHL9 causes autosomal dominant early-onset distal myopathy with areflexia and sensory involvement, so it is a close second. Keloids, loss of consciousness, esotropia, kyphosis and galactose intolerance are non-specific. The negative findings (no alpha-dystroglycan hypoglycosylation, no intellectual disability, no optic atrophy, no neonatal diabetes, no visual loss) argue against LARGE1, DDOST, OPA3, KCNJ11, RAB3GAP1, ADAM9 and the other candidates. PIGA, ATP6AP2, LGALS1, SOST and LZTFL1 do not fit this neuromuscular phenotype.

30078.Rationale: Childhood-onset distal weakness, steppage gait, axonal neuropathy, myopathic EMG and mixed seizures (absence, focal, myoclonic) fit a neurodegenerative or lysosomal/mitochondrial disorder. HEXB (GM2 gangliosidosis, juvenile Sandhoff) can cause motor neuropathy or neuronopathy with seizures, and it carries a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 40. MT-TE is a known cause of mitochondrial myopathy/neuropathy with epilepsy, but its variant has weak support (PP2=0), so it ranks second. TPP1 (CLN2/SCAR7) causes seizures and neurodegeneration but no variant is observed. GBA2 and MTPAP cause spastic ataxia or paraplegia, and spasticity and ataxia are marked absent. The remaining genes are linked to unrelated phenotypes (cataract, ectodermal dysplasia, hypogonadism, etc.) and have no neuromuscular or epilepsy link. This ranking comes from my own recall of the literature. I did not run any searches or database lookups, and I could not identify what Disease ID 399081 refers to.

38573.Rationale: Childhood-onset distal-predominant peripheral axonal neuropathy with intrinsic hand muscle weakness and atrophy, absent Achilles and patellar reflexes, ankle contractures, and myopathic EMG changes fits the dominant intermediate or axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth spectrum caused by DNM2 (CMT-DIB and CMT2M). DNM2 also carries a rare, high-CADD splice and missense variant. The phenotypes recorded as absent (spasticity, ataxia, ALS, cerebellar signs, proximal amyotrophy, and centrally nucleated fibers) argue against the other neuromuscular candidates: ATXN3 (SCA3), GBA2 (spastic paraplegia and ataxia), NEB (nemaline myopathy), and the myopathy genes. MT-TE (mitochondrial myopathy and neuropathy, tRNA-Glu) is a plausible second candidate, but the absent skeletal myopathy and absent PEO or diabetes weigh against it. The remaining genes have no clear link to the phenotype. This ranking rests on my own recall of the literature and I did not run any searches.

41362.Rationale: Severe short stature (HP:0003510) is the most specific, gene-informative phenotype and it points to GHR (growth hormone insensitivity/Laron syndrome). GHR is also onset in childhood and carries a rare, high-CADD (36) splice/missense variant. NSMCE2 (primordial dwarfism with insulin resistance and gonadal failure) and CDCA7 (ICF syndrome with growth and facial dysmorphism such as low-set ears) are the next-best fits for growth failure with dysmorphism. TSHB (central hypothyroidism) is a weaker growth-related candidate. The remaining genes are cardiovascular/lipid (CETP, SCARB1, PON3, SERPINC1), renal/ion channel (PKHD1, SCNN1B), neuromuscular (MPZ, MYH14, MYH7B), ciliary (DNAH11), or immune genes with no clear link to the cataract, nystagmus, ataxia, microcornea and anhidrosis features. CHM and AVP have no observed variant. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of the genes, not from a literature search or database lookup run in this session.

5344.Rationale: Infant-onset seizures with hypsarrhythmia (infantile spasms), developmental regression, intellectual disability, hypotonia/poor head control, feeding difficulty and nystagmus/optic atrophy point to a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. GABRB2 (GABA-A receptor beta-2 subunit) is a known cause of DEE (DEE92) with infantile spasms, regression, and visual involvement, and the candidate variant is a high-CADD (36) rare splice/missense change. POGZ (White-Sutton syndrome: ID, feeding problems, vision abnormalities, seizures) and GLS2 (recently reported neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy/hypotonia) are the next best fits. OPA3 and ELP1 explain only isolated features (optic atrophy; hyporeflexia/autonomic dysfunction). The other genes (GATA3, TTPA, CPT2, TXNRD2, RPGRIP1, KIT, CYP7A1, HTR5A, SIK1, PDIA2) have weak or no match to the core epileptic-encephalopathy phenotype. This ranking is from recalled knowledge only. I did not run any literature searches or lookups.

22975.Rationale: Reasoned from the phenotype list and gene knowledge only. I did no literature or web search, and I could not identify what Disease ID 654 refers to. HbH hemoglobin (HP:0011903) is the most specific finding. It points to ATRX, the cause of alpha-thalassemia X-linked intellectual disability, where HbH inclusions occur. ATRX also has the highest CADD score (54) and a splice/missense variant. Orofacial cleft is also reported in ATRX syndrome. 6722.Rationale: The picture is early-onset non-progressive cerebellar ataxia (gait and truncal), cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, nystagmus, dysarthria, global developmental delay with moderate intellectual disability, dystonia and kinetic tremor. Scores are from recalled gene-disease associations; no literature search was run.

7041.Rationale: Answer is from recall; I ran no literature search. Disease ID 521445 was not looked up. 13619.Rationale: Not verified against the literature or the web; this ranking comes from recall of gene-phenotype associations only. KDM2B is ranked first. 24818.Rationale: Answer is from recall of the literature; I ran no searches. 16667.Rationale: Infant-onset global developmental delay, intellectual disability, speech delay, hypotonia, ataxia, seizures, decreased head circumference, abnormal forehead, failure to thrive, GERD, short stature, and aggressive or self-injurious behavior best match DYRK1A syndrome (MRD7). 39576.Rationale: No literature or database lookups were run. The ranking comes from prior knowledge of gene-phenotype associations. 22680.Rationale: Ranked from recalled knowledge of gene-disease associations only; I ran no literature or database searches. 35675.Rationale: Answer is from recall of the literature, with no search run. 7944.Rationale: Answered from recalled literature only; no searches were run. FLNA best fits the profile. Gain-of-function FLNA variants cause the otopalatodigital/frontometaphyseal spectrum: increased bone density, joint contractures and ankylosis, congenital heart defects including AV canal defect, and GI involvement (which could explain the melena). 34238.Rationale: The phenotype set fits HSD10 mitochondrial disease (HSD17B10, X-linked): childhood onset, choreoathetosis, hyperkinetic movements, ataxia, gait disturbance, mixed seizure types (focal, absence, myoclonic), visual impairment, and behavioral problems including psychosis and hyperactivity. 22506.Rationale: Phenotype of childhood-onset choreoathetosis/hyperkinetic movements, ataxia, intellectual disability, abnormal speech, hyperactivity, visual impairment, glucose intolerance and decreased liver function, with ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, neuropathy and hearing loss absent, best fits HSD10 disease (HSD17B10, X-linked; a mitochondrial RNase P/ISB metabolism defect). 8556.Rationale: Answered from memory only; no literature search was run. Disease ID 67047 was not identified. The phenotype set looks like a mix of unrelated features. MICOS13 (C19orf70) deficiency causes hepatoencephalopathy with mitochondrial dysfunction and liver disease, so it ranks first. The list names it twice, as MICOS13 and as C19orf70. Only the C19orf70 entry has an observed variant, so it is scored slightly higher. PNPLA2 is a neutral lipid storage gene closely related to the Chanarin-Dorfman pathway (ichthyosis, hepatosplenomegaly, intellectual disability, ataxia), which gives a partial fit. ABCC8 encodes the KATP channel SUR1 subunit, and its pathogenic variants cause permanent or transient neonatal diabetes. It is also the only candidate with a strong, specific link to the core phenotype. Its variant is a high-CADD splice/missense change. The remaining genes are ranked lower on weaker links. 16854.Rationale: Answered from phenotype-to-gene knowledge, with no literature or database search run. Disease ID 2680 was not looked up. The profile is infant-onset with diarrhea, cachexia (failure to thrive), hepatic involvement, hypotonia, seizures, and premature ovarian insufficiency. That combination fits classic galactosemia (GALT): premature ovarian insufficiency is a hallmark long-term complication, and neonatal diarrhea, wasting and liver disease are typical. GALT also carries a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 37. AMPD2 (pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 9 with infantile seizures, hypotonia and abnormal reflexes) is the second-best fit for the neurological features. SACS (spastic ataxia with abnormal EMG and reflexes) and CHN1 (neurodevelopmental/motor) are weaker neurological fits. LGI4 (peripheral nerve myelination, hypotonia and joint limitation in arthrogryposis models), TMPRSS6 and MVD are weak. The remaining genes have no clear link to this phenotype set. F8 and F8A1 have no observed variant. The bare identifier 340451 in the candidate list is not a gene symbol, so it is left out of the ranking.

19531.Rationale: Infantile-onset hypotonia, areflexia/reduced tendon reflexes, abnormal EMG, respiratory distress, feeding difficulty and multiple joint contractures point to a congenital (hypomyelinating) neuropathy or neurogenic arthrogryposis. MPZ is the classic gene for congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy and severe early-onset CMT (Dejerine-Sottas). This ranking comes from recalled knowledge only. I did not run a literature search and did not check Disease ID 2680 against any database.

12542.Rationale: Answered from phenotype matching and recalled knowledge only; I ran no literature search. 37963.Rationale: This ranking comes from my own knowledge. I did no literature or web search and could not identify what Disease ID 2680 refers to. 9783.Rationale: Answer is from recall only; I did no literature search and no web search. The 'Disease ID: 777' was not resolved to a named disorder. The patient has a neurodevelopmental phenotype (moderate ID, autism, obesity) with mild dysmorphism (thick lower lip, long palpebral fissures, depressed nasal bridge, delayed tooth eruption, 2-3 toe syndactyly, short distal phalanges). They also have a hemostatic and vascular signature (prolonged bleeding time, thromboembolism, vascular dilatation, miosis). That combination fits the platelet and vascular features plus ID and autism best, so I rank it first. The absent features (macrocephaly, short stature, webbed neck, low-set ears, sparse hair) look like the Noonan-like picture of PPP1CB, and the absent thickened skin and lymphangioma look like the Proteus picture of AKT1. These absences count against both genes, so they rank next, below RAP1A. The remaining genes are known for unrelated phenotypes: LSS (hypotrichosis, cataract, alopecia-intellectual disability), BSND (Bartter syndrome with deafness), CAPN3 (limb-girdle muscular dystrophy), SYNE1 (ataxia and muscular dystrophy), and PCDHA6, TSPYL1 and USP27X (weak or X-linked ID candidates). I scored these low.

26794.Rationale: The picture is infantile hypotonia, feeding difficulty, seizures, arthrogryposis and flexion contractures, developmental delay, and a facial gestalt of open mouth, full cheeks, short nose, epicanthus and macrotia. ATRX carries a rare splice/missense variant with a very high CADD of 54, so it is the clear top candidate. Other candidates have no strong match to this phenotype set. CTNND1 (blepharocheilodontic syndrome, with some ocular and developmental features) and GNAQ (Sturge-Weber/vascular, but nevus flammeus is absent) are only weak matches. This ranking comes from prior knowledge, with no literature search run.

Loss-of-function and missense variants cause episodic ataxia type 1 (EA1) with myokymia, and also cause myoclonus and ataxia, which are two of the positive phenotypes. CNPY3 is associated with epileptic encephalopathy but does not fit well here. This ranking is from prior knowledge, with no literature search run.

15748.Rationale: Answered from recall of the literature; no database or web lookup was run. The skeletal core of the phenotype (abnormal vertebral bodies, abnormal intervertebral discs, short thorax, short stature, IUGR) matches a spondylocostal dysostosis / segmentation-defect picture, and RIPPLY2 is the somitogenesis gene among the candidates (SCDO6). 17852.Rationale: Answered from prior knowledge only; no literature search or database lookup was run, and the match of Disease ID 98892 to a specific disorder is not confirmed. The phenotype is a connective-tissue/vascular pattern: joint hypermobility, patellar dislocation, early knee osteoarthritis, scoliosis, hernia, valve and great-artery malformations, and abnormal bleeding. XYLT2 (glycosaminoglycan synthesis; spondylo-ocular syndrome, with an EDS-like spectrum including cardiac valve defects and hernia) fits best. Osteoporosis and skeletal dysplasia are listed as absent, so the match is imperfect. NOTCH2 is second: Alagille syndrome 2 involves congenital great-vessel and cardiac malformations and bleeding, and Hajdu-Cheney is argued against by the absent osteoporosis. LRP4 and HNRNPA2B1 are weaker skeletal or multisystem possibilities. HNRNPA2B1 has the highest CADD but its disease phenotype (multisystem proteinopathy) does not match. The remaining genes (AUH, GJB3, PLEKHM1, MTG1, CLCN5, NEDD4L, AHNAK, LRRC7) have disease associations that fit poorly, so they are ranked low.
