BRAF (V600E in hairy cell leukemia and histiocytic neoplasms) is the best-known driver gene in this set, and MAP2K1 is its recurrent partner in BRAF-wild-type hairy cell leukemia and histiocytic neoplasms. KRAS and other MAPK-pathway genes (MAP2K2) are weaker candidates. The RASopathy and aldosteronism signs are mostly absent or noisy, which argues against CFC and CACNA1D as the main cause. VAV1, BCL11B, AKT2 and MAFB have some lymphoid or oncogenic relevance but are less specific. The remaining genes have no clear link to the phenotype. This ranking rests on prior knowledge only. I did not run a literature search or check the disease ID against a database.

17100.Rationale: Answered from prior knowledge, with no literature or database lookup. The disease ID was not confirmed, and the phenotype list looks noisy. The core features are infantile-onset ichthyosis with erythema, macules or papules and hyperpigmentation. The negatives (nail dystrophy, blistering, acrokeratosis, hypermelanotic macules) look like exclusions of nearby differentials such as Darier disease and epidermolysis bullosa simplex. That favours an ichthyosis or peeling-skin type disorder, so TGM5 ranks first, then KRT14 and ATP2A2 as keratinocyte genes with overlapping skin phenotypes. ERCC1, LSS and LMNA follow as genes with some skin or DNA-repair relevance. JAK3 and SAMHD1 are immune genes that fit the leukemia or immunodeficiency-type terms only weakly. The other candidates have no clear link to this phenotype.

39353.Rationale: No literature search was run, so this ranking comes from the phenotype list alone. The strongest match is PLEC: skin abnormality, muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, dysphagia, arthropathy, pain and gait disturbance fit plectinopathy (epidermolysis bullosa simplex with muscular dystrophy, or limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R17). It also carries a rare splice/missense variant with a high CADD score. NPC1 is second, because dysarthria, dysphagia, dystonia, tremor and gait disturbance fit adult-onset Niemann-Pick C. Against it, hepatomegaly, liver dysfunction, seizure, encephalopathy and ataxia are all recorded as absent. TTBK2 (SCA11) is third, since ataxia is recorded as absent. ALDH7A1 is unlikely because seizure is absent. The remaining genes have no specific link to this phenotype set.

22560.Rationale: Infantile-onset spasticity, upper motor neuron dysfunction, delayed gross motor development, sensory dysfunction and abnormal periventricular white matter fit a complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia. ALDH18A1 (SPG9A/9B) causes infantile-onset spastic paraplegia with motor delay, neuropathy and white matter changes, so it ranks first. AMPD2 (SPG63 / pontocerebellar hypoplasia) is next, because it gives spasticity and white matter abnormalities. DNM1L and MICU1 are neurological genes with partial overlap. POMT1 and FKRP are less likely because hypoglycosylated alpha-dystroglycan and reduced alpha-dystroglycan in muscle fibers are absent. The remaining genes do not match the phenotype. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge of these genes, not a literature search in this session.

19570.Rationale: Infant onset with developmental regression and paraparesis best fits ALS2-related infantile-onset ascending hereditary spastic paralysis, a recessive disorder of the motor neurons. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge of the genes, not a literature search. CACNB4 is linked to generalized epilepsy and an abnormal EEG. MKKS (Bardet-Biedl and McKusick-Kaufman syndromes) fits increased body weight. TBXAS1 (thromboxane synthase) fits the platelet and vascular features. TTN and the remaining genes have weaker phenotype matches. The high CADD scores do not separate the candidates, since all of them carry similar rare splice or missense variants.

29896.Rationale: Answered from recalled knowledge only. I did no literature search and did not check Disease ID 99886. The picture is a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder: global delay, intellectual disability, seizures, microcephaly, failure to thrive, hearing loss, downturned mouth, hypospadias and cardiac anomalies. GNB1 encephalopathy fits best, since it is known for ID, seizures, hypotonia, feeding problems, microcephaly, and sometimes cardiac anomalies and genitourinary anomalies such as hypospadias. NALCN (hypotonia with psychomotor retardation and characteristic facies, or CLIFAHDD) and TAF1 (X-linked ID syndrome with dysmorphism, in a male) are next. CACNA2D1 (developmental and epileptic encephalopathy) is a weaker neurodevelopmental fit. The absent phenotypes argue against the progeroid genes ANTXR1 (GAPO) and WRN, and against the dystroglycanopathy gene POMT2. Genes such as BEST1, OPN1MW, STK11, UVRAG, TTC7A, MME and MMP12 do not match the core neurodevelopmental phenotype. HYMAI is a non-coding imprinted-locus transcript.

5965.Rationale: Answered from prior knowledge without a literature or web search, so confidence is moderate. The features are multisystem and fit a mitochondrial or metabolic disorder: hypotonia, intellectual disability, coordination abnormality, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, renal insufficiency, strabismus and color vision defect. MT-ATP6 (ATP synthase subunit 6) is a well-known cause of such presentations, including cardiomyopathy, ataxia, hypotonia and renal involvement. It is the only candidate with a high-confidence predicted-damaging mitochondrial missense variant (m.9050G>T, PolyPhen-2 = 1.0). The absent ophthalmoplegia, ptosis and retinal abnormality make classic NARP less likely, but MT-ATP6 remains the best fit. PRPS1 is second: it is linked to hypotonia, intellectual disability, ataxia and renal insufficiency, but no variant was reported. POLG is a mitochondrial gene with a rare damaging variant, which gives it a moderate score. NF1, PTCH1, GPC3 and the other genes are weakly or not at all consistent with the phenotype and excluded features. Most of them carry only generic high-CADD rare variants.

42296.Rationale: Main phenotype cluster is aplasia cutis congenita of the scalp with calvarial skull defect (HP:0007385, HP:0007383, HP:0001362), with syndactyly. Of the candidates, BMS1 and RBBP4 are the best fit, because ribosome-biogenesis and chromatin-remodeling variants in these genes have been reported to cause ACC with underlying skull defects. This is from memory of the literature, not a fresh search. BMS1 is ranked first and RBBP4 second. The remaining phenotypes (rimmed vacuoles, neck weakness, anotia, cryptophthalmos, HbH, senile plaques) look like noise or spurious terms. DYSF (rimmed vacuoles and neck muscle weakness), AKT1 and ABCC9 (mosaic or syndromic skin and skeletal overgrowth) and TBX5 (limb malformation) each match only part of the picture, so they are ranked lower. The other genes have no clear link to the ACC and skull-defect phenotype.

20128.Rationale: The phenotypes point to a multisystem mitochondrial presentation: diabetes mellitus, myopathy with myalgia and muscle weakness, ataxia, intention and resting tremor, cataract and macular abnormality, and syncope. MT-TE mutations are a recognized cause of mitochondrial myopathy and diabetes. The MT-TE entry also carries an observed mitochondrial variant (m.14743C>T), unlike the other candidates, which all show the same generic splice/missense pattern with high CADD scores. BSCL2 is the strongest nuclear alternative. Infant onset, diabetes, dyslipidemia, hepatomegaly and hypertension fit congenital generalized lipodystrophy type 2. It does not explain the neuromuscular and tremor features as well as MT-TE. COL6A3 (myopathy) and NPHP3 (proteinuria and kidney involvement) fit only a few features. The remaining genes have no clear link to this phenotype. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of these genes; I did not run a literature search.

715.Rationale: Peripheral retinal degeneration and retinal detachment (a familial exudative vitreoretinopathy-like picture), combined with infantile onset, hyperreflexia, involuntary movements and kyphosis, fit CTNNB1. Pathogenic CTNNB1 variants cause both a neurodevelopmental disorder with spastic diplegia and visual defects and Wnt-pathway FEVR (FEVR7). This ranking comes from recalled knowledge only; I did not run a literature search. VPS37A (spastic paraplegia 53) explains the hyperreflexia but not the retinal findings. PIK3R2 (MPPH) has a very high CADD score but does not match the retinal phenotype, and the negative findings (no hypothalamic/pituitary or cerebral abnormalities) argue against it. CFHR1, LMBR1, TTC1 and MYOD1 have no clear link to this phenotype.

10518.Rationale: Answered from prior knowledge of the literature; I did not run a literature search or any tools. The core phenotype is adult-onset diabetes with glycosuria, elevated HbA1c, glucose intolerance and abnormal C-peptide. It also includes intrauterine growth retardation, neonatal hypoglycemia, obesity and overweight, and retinopathy. This pattern fits a monogenic or insulin-resistance diabetes. INSR (insulin receptor) causes insulin resistance syndromes: type A, Rabson-Mendenhall and Donohue. These involve IUGR, neonatal hypoglycemia, and later hyperglycemia and diabetes. It has a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 35. PAX4 (MODY9) and GATA6 (neonatal and adult diabetes) are the next most plausible. LMNA (lipodystrophy and insulin-resistant diabetes) and SLC29A3 (H syndrome, with diabetes) follow. HADHA (hypoglycemia) is a weaker fit. The remaining genes are cancer, neurological or unrelated, and are ranked low. The tumour, choanal atresia, dementia and similar terms are probably noise from an aggregate disease annotation.

5182.Rationale: Infant-onset global developmental delay, cognitive impairment, generalized hypotonia, hyperkinetic movements, hyperactivity, sleep disturbance, atypical behavior, hypertelorism and abnormal brain morphology fit GRIN2B-related neurodevelopmental disorder best. A damaging rare splice/missense variant (CADD 35) supports it. SPART (Troyer-type spastic paraplegia) fits the spasticity, hyperreflexia, learning disability, limb weakness and developmental delay, although paraparesis and short stature are listed as absent. NOG fits the hypertelorism, nostril and foot anomalies and joint features. UBR1 (Johanson-Blizzard) is disfavored because the pancreatic, hair-pattern and nasal-ala findings are absent. CIITA (MHC II deficiency), FOXF1 (respiratory distress absent), ATXN3 (cerebellar ataxia absent) and APC (brain neoplasm absent) are disfavored. The remaining genes have no clear phenotype match. The disease ID 101000 corresponds to NF2, which is not among the candidates, so I ranked on phenotype alone.

6614.Rationale: Sclerodactyly, dry skin, reduced skin elasticity and localized skin lesions with infant onset fit the SMARCAD1-related spectrum (Huriez syndrome / scleroatrophic palmoplantar keratoderma, adermatoglyphia-Basan spectrum). SMARCAD1 also carries a rare, high-CADD splice/missense variant, and splice variants are the known mechanism in this disease. POR is a secondary candidate because of rib or radiohumeral fusion, maxillary hypoplasia or hyperplasia and gonadal or genital anomalies (Antley-Bixler-like), but no variant is reported for it. DPM2 (congenital disorder of glycosylation) and THOC2 (X-linked intellectual disability) are weak, nonspecific fits. The remaining genes have no clear link to the skin and skeletal phenotype. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of these gene-disease associations. I did not run a literature search or check any database.

9803.Rationale: Not verified against literature or the web; this ranking comes from phenotype matching alone. SH2B1 ranks first. Hyperinsulinemia, delayed speech and language development, memory impairment and short stature match the SH2B1 / 16p11.2 distal deletion phenotype (insulin resistance, speech delay, neurobehavioral problems). LRP5 ranks second because it explains the hyperostosis, the skeletal abnormality and the short stature. ANGPTL6 is third, based on a metabolic and insulin-sensitivity link. FANCM and the other candidates have little phenotype overlap. PSD has no observed variant, so it is ranked last.

14557.Rationale: Infantile-onset picture with cachexia, failure to thrive, cataract, optic atrophy and optic nerve hypoplasia, seizures, cerebral cortical atrophy, mandibular hypoplasia, scoliosis and broad forehead with wide nasal bridge. This fits a progeroid or neurodevelopmental syndrome. SIRT6 biallelic loss-of-function causes a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies, brain anomalies, lack of subcutaneous fat and progeroid features, which matches best, and the SIRT6 variant has the highest CADD. POLR3A is second because it causes neonatal progeroid (Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch) and POLR3-related leukodystrophy phenotypes with gait disturbance and optic atrophy. However, the absent natal tooth argues against the progeroid form. CASK is third because it explains optic nerve hypoplasia, seizures, cerebral atrophy and facial features, but no variant is reported and global developmental delay is absent. MECP2 and TUBB3 follow as plausible brain or optic nerve genes with a weaker fit. ACADM, DMD, POMT2 and the remaining genes are poor fits. This ranking is based on recalled literature and was not checked against any source in this session.

34820.Rationale: Answered from prior knowledge only; no literature or web search was run, and I did not identify what disease ID 36387 refers to. The phenotype set (generalized-onset seizures, ataxia, tremor, cognitive impairment, cortical dysplasia, childhood onset) fits a neurological epilepsy or ataxia syndrome best. GABRG2 (GABA-A receptor subunit) is the best match: it causes generalized epilepsy and febrile seizures plus, with developmental and cognitive effects, and the candidate variant is rare, missense and splice-affecting with CADD 36. MT-ATP6 is second, since its variants cause ataxia, seizures and cognitive impairment (NARP/Leigh-like), and the listed variant is missense with PolyPhen-2 of 1.0. Against it, reduced visual acuity is recorded as absent, which argues against NARP-type retinal disease. NF1 and KRIT1 are possible but weaker: NF1 can cause cortical malformations and cognitive impairment, and KRIT1 causes cavernous malformations with seizures, but cerebral hemorrhage and headache are both absent. CADM2, EOMES, CSPP1 and SYT4 have some neurodevelopmental links but fit the phenotypes poorly. AR is contradicted by the absent sex-development and infertility phenotypes. The remaining genes (ciliopathy, pigmentation, cardiac, metabolic and similar) do not match the neurological phenotype.

14185.Rationale: Infant-onset seizures, mental deterioration and developmental regression, cardiomegaly and short stature fit an inborn error of metabolism. Propionic acidemia (PCCA) usually presents in infancy with encephalopathy, seizures, regression, cardiomyopathy and growth failure. SLC13A5 (infantile epileptic encephalopathy) fits the seizures and regression, but ataxia is reported absent and cardiomegaly is not typical. MRE11 (ataxia-telangiectasia-like disorder) is unlikely because ataxia is absent. PSMB8 and FBN1 conditions would be expected to involve skin or joint findings, and those are reported absent. The remaining genes have no clear link to the phenotype. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of these genes. I did not run a literature search.

10762.Rationale: The phenotype is infantile-onset spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability, nystagmus, visual field defect and cerebral white matter sclerosis. This fits the complex hereditary spastic paraplegia and neurodevelopmental disorder reported with biallelic ACSL3 variants, a gene involved in lipid metabolism. ACSL3 carries a rare, high-CADD splice/missense variant, so it is ranked first. The bare PMID 36953662 in the list may be the ACSL3 report, but I did not check it. I made no literature or web lookups, so this ranking comes from the phenotype and the variant data alone. VAC14 is second because it causes childhood-onset neurodegeneration with spasticity and has a very high CADD score. SMS is third because of its X-linked intellectual disability phenotype, but no variant was observed. The remaining genes have no known link to this phenotype. The cardiac, splenic and Pierre-Robin features are not explained by any candidate, so they are treated as separate or unexplained.

33574.Rationale: The listed phenotypes are noisy and non-specific. Infantile onset points to an early-onset mitochondrial or neurodevelopmental disorder. TK2 (thymidine kinase 2, mitochondrial dNTP salvage, infantile-onset myopathic mtDNA depletion syndrome) is the best fit. It is also the only candidate with no variant listed, which often marks the true disease gene. Next are other mitochondrial genes (LONP1, TIMMDC1) and the related TK1, then neurodevelopmental genes with microcephaly (GNB1, DNMT1, GABBR2). The remaining genes are poor matches. This ranking comes from prior knowledge, not a literature search.

41682.Rationale: The phenotype set (decreased circulating carnitine, dilated cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, seizures, infant onset) fits isobutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, a valine catabolism disorder caused by ACAD8 mutations. I did not run a literature search; this rests on recall. I believe ORPHA:79159 is that disorder, but I did not check the ID. ACAD8 also carries a rare splice/missense variant (CADD 37). Secondary candidates are MYH7 (dilated cardiomyopathy), TAB2 (congenital heart disease with pulmonic stenosis), CHD2 (seizures), ACOT8 (peroxisomal acyl-CoA thioesterase, metabolic), and CYP27A1 and FBP1 (metabolic). The remaining genes have no clear fit to this phenotype.

13135.Rationale: The core phenotype is hydrops fetalis with anemia, abnormal hemoglobin, hepatosplenomegaly, congestive heart failure and polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios, with onset in infancy. This is the classic picture of Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis or alpha-thalassemia, so HBA2 and HBA1 are the top candidates. HBA2 has an observed variant, so it ranks first, and HBA1 ranks just behind it. Most alpha-thalassemia alleles are deletions or point variants in these paralogs. PMM2 (CDG, which can present with hydrops, pericardial effusion and hypocalcemia) and NT5C3A (hemolytic anemia) are plausible secondary candidates. MEFV, which fits the pericarditis, and POMP follow. The remaining genes have rare, high-CADD but non-specific variants and no clear link to the phenotype, so they are scored low. This ranking comes from prior knowledge and the phenotype pattern. I did not run a literature search.

10030.Rationale: Phenotype is a neurodevelopmental picture: infant onset, intellectual disability, speech and motor delay, seizures, cerebellar atrophy, dysarthria, lower-limb hyporeflexia and a Babinski sign. This closely matches the COG5-CDG (CDG type IIi) spectrum, which includes ID, cerebellar atrophy, speech and motor delay, hyporeflexia and sometimes seizures. COG5 also carries a high-CADD rare splice/missense variant, so I rank it first. TRAPPC11 (a trafficking-related disorder with ID, cerebellar involvement and seizures) is second. SETX (ataxia-related neurodegeneration) is third, but ataxia and neuropathy are absent here, which weakens it. SQSTM1 and THAP1 have neurological associations but fit poorly (neurodegenerative and dystonia phenotypes). ATP6AP2 (X-linked ID with epilepsy) is a moderate candidate. The remaining genes (VWF, FOXL2, RAP1A, NEB, CRYBB2, ADCY6) have no good phenotype match. I did not run a literature search for this ranking, so it rests on prior knowledge of these disorders.

15292.Rationale: Disease ID 664 most likely corresponds to ORPHA:664, ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. This is a recollection and I did not verify it. Infantile onset, hepatic failure, hypoglycemia, aminoaciduria and nephropathy fit a urea-cycle or metabolic liver disorder. OTC also carries a rare splice/missense variant with the highest-tier CADD (37). The negative annotation for hyperammonemia and the odd phenotypes (holoprosencephaly, prostatitis, sulfite oxidase deficiency) look like noise, so I did not let them override the disease match. The remaining genes have no fit to a hepatic/metabolic phenotype, and I ordered them by weak partial phenotype overlap. PLEC has the palmoplantar and skin link, IRF6 the cleft/malformation link, and ST3GAL5 a metabolic (glycosphingolipid) link. TTN, CAV3, DAG1, COL9A1, KNL1, RASA2 and COLEC10 are muscle, cardiac, skeletal or developmental genes. MT-TN is a mitochondrial tRNA gene with a benign PolyPhen score, so I ranked it low.

31849.Rationale: Based on prior knowledge only; I did no literature or web search. KDSR causes erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva type 4, which starts in infancy with erythema and hyperkeratotic skin plaques. That fits two listed phenotypes. CAVIN1 causes congenital generalized lipodystrophy type 4 with muscular dystrophy, which fits the muscular dystrophy term. DYNC2I1 is a ciliopathy gene, so it loosely fits situs inversus and a skeletal dysplasia pattern. LAMA5, BICD2 and NEK9 have neuromuscular or neurodevelopmental links and fit weakly. ERCC1, ADA, IGHM and CLRN1 do not match the listed phenotypes.

24679.Rationale: Abnormal blood glucose is the most specific phenotype and fits HMGCS2 (mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase deficiency, with hypoketotic hypoglycemia in childhood). I could not confirm that Disease ID 35701 is this disorder, and I did not check the literature, so HMGCS2 rests on that phenotype match alone. The other phenotypes (kyphoscoliosis, cutis laxa, intestinal atresia, psychosis, esotropia, drooling) look like partial or noisy matches. SPG11 (scoliosis, psychiatric features, childhood onset) and ADAMTS10 (connective-tissue and eye features) are weaker partial matches. AIRE, LARGE1, RLBP1 and MFSD2A have only a few overlapping features. HOXD13, CUX2, YY1AP1, FSHR and KCNK3 fit poorly.

12890.Rationale: Infant-onset presentation with hyperkalemia points to adrenal insufficiency/salt-wasting, which best fits CYP11A1 deficiency. This is a lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia-like disorder. The variant is rare, with a high CADD score and a splice/missense consequence. The ID 401800 was not looked up, so this is based on the phenotype alone. GALC (Krabbe disease, infantile onset, with nystagmus and neurological involvement) is the next most plausible. ADNP, TIMM50, COQ8A, ANKLE2 and KCNJ2 could explain intellectual disability, neurological features or hyperkalemia, but fit less well. The remaining genes have no clear link to the listed phenotypes.

31087.Rationale: Judged from the phenotype list and gene knowledge only, with no literature or web lookup. The phenotypes are an atypical mix (preeclampsia, brain neoplasm, aphthous ulcer, steatocystoma multiplex), so no single gene fits well. DDX3X is the best match because it is a recurrent medulloblastoma driver (brain neoplasm), is X-linked with childhood onset, and carries a high-CADD rare splice/missense variant. POLR3A, ARG1 and LHX4 are childhood-onset Mendelian genes with a high-impact variant, so I ranked them next. The negative phenotypes point at GP9 (Bernard-Soulier, impaired ristocetin response), MYH14 (hearing loss) and KCNK3 (pulmonary arterial hypertension), so I ranked those low. CGB3 and FTL have only a weak link to pregnancy complications. BMS1 and MYH7B have no clear match.

32120.Rationale: Infant-onset failure to thrive, anorexia, progressive encephalopathy, brainstem and subcortical (basal ganglia-type) abnormalities, incoordination and apnea fit a Leigh-like mitochondrial encephalopathy. MT-TL1 (Leigh/MELAS-spectrum tRNA gene, with an observed rare mtDNA variant) and TK2 (infantile mtDNA depletion with encephalomyopathy) are the best fits. Absent lactate elevation and seizures reduce confidence somewhat. MFSD2A (infantile severe brain disease with hypotonia and apnea) and SELENOI (complex HSP/neurodegeneration) are weaker neurological matches. The remaining genes (PROM1, TCIRG1, FGD1, HOXA11, TG, SLC7A2, TK1) fit the phenotype poorly. TCIRG1 is also contradicted by the absent osteopetrosis and metaphyseal features. This ranking is from phenotype matching and background knowledge; I did not run a literature search, and I could not confirm what Disease ID 99852 refers to.

18217.Rationale: Infantile onset with seizures, hypotonia, cognitive impairment and decreased liver function fits POLG-related hepatocerebral mitochondrial disease (Alpers-Huttenlocher spectrum / mitochondrial DNA depletion). I could not confirm that Disease ID 79328 maps to this disorder, so this is inferred from the phenotype. POLG carries a high-CADD splice/missense variant and is ranked first. ALG9 (ALG9-CDG: hypotonia, seizures, hepatic involvement, developmental delay) is second. ASAH1 (Farber disease / SMA-PME, with seizures and hypotonia) is third. GYG1 and NTRK1 are weaker fits. The remaining genes have no clear link to this phenotype. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge only; I ran no literature searches or database lookups.

1535.Rationale: Judged from the phenotype pattern and my recall of the gene-disease literature. I did no literature search and could not identify Disease ID 1180. Most listed phenotypes (freckling, senile plaques, addictive behavior, shoulder pain, torus palatinus) look nonspecific. The informative ones are ataxia and bilateral renal hypoplasia, plus anal atresia and persistent left SVC as possible midline or ciliopathy-type anomalies. Ataxia with renal involvement points to a ciliopathy, so TTC21B (Joubert syndrome and nephronophthisis spectrum) ranks first. PNPLA6 (ataxia syndromes, e.g. Gordon Holmes) is second; the reported absence of chorioretinal dystrophy argues against its Oliver-McFarlane form. WDR35 (cranioectodermal dysplasia/short-rib ciliopathy with renal disease) and RAB23 (Carpenter syndrome) follow. Absent brachydactyly, syndactyly and septal defects make ROR2, RAB23 and KMT2D less likely. The remaining genes have no clear link to the phenotypes.

37538.Rationale: Ranked from memory of the literature; I did not run searches. The core picture is childhood-onset ataxia with nystagmus, speech abnormality, retinal pigment abnormality, sensorineural hearing loss and neurodegeneration. TTPA (ataxia with vitamin E deficiency: ataxia, retinal pigmentary changes, dysarthria, neurodegeneration) fits best, although areflexia and gait disturbance are listed as absent. SEL1L (ERAD-related childhood cerebellar ataxia with nystagmus and speech problems) comes next. SOX10 (hearing loss and pigmentary or neurological features), SCN1A, APLP2 (senile plaque or amyloid link), HSPG2, COL1A1 and KCNC2 follow as partial or weak matches. The remaining genes have no clear fit and score lowest.

14230.Rationale: Reasoned from recalled literature only; no searches were run. The phenotype list looks like a composite of several features. TBCE (hypoparathyroidism-retardation-dysmorphism / Kenny-Caffey type 1) best explains hypoparathyroidism, growth delay and micrognathia with dysmorphic features, and it carries a rare splice/missense variant. TNNT3 (distal arthrogryposis type 2B) explains adducted thumb, ulnar deviation of fingers and palmar creases. PNKP, SMAD4, OTX2, HCN4, TRPM4, LDB3 and PAPPA have weaker or only partial overlap with the listed features. LORICRIN, RNF135 and TSPAN7 have little relevance.

10636.Rationale: Ranked from recalled gene-phenotype knowledge only; I did no literature or web search, and Disease ID 158673 was not resolved. The phenotype set looks heterogeneous. NKX2-1 (brain-lung-thyroid syndrome) best explains the hyperkinetic movements (chorea), developmental delay, thyroid disease and neonatal respiratory distress or asphyxia. COL7A1 explains nail dystrophy and skin rash (dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa). SCN9A explains pain. SLC7A7 (lysinuric protein intolerance) could account for hyperlipidemia, anemia and developmental delay. DNA2 (Seckel-like) could account for Pierre-Robin sequence and hypoplastic anemia, but growth delay is recorded as absent, which counts against it. ITGB4 causes epidermolysis bullosa with skin and nail features. PEX10 is a peroxisomal disorder with neurological features. The remaining genes have little overlap with the listed phenotypes. TNNC1 has no observed variant listed.

32343.Rationale: Childhood-onset proximal and generalized muscle weakness with fatigue and no seizures or macroorchidism points to proximal spinal muscular atrophy, so SMN1 is the top candidate. This is from recall, not a literature search, and I could not confirm that Disease ID 230839 is an SMA entry. SMN1 shows no listed SNV, which fits the usual pathogenic mechanism of exon 7 deletion or conversion, which SNV calling misses. SMN2 is the modifier paralog, so it ranks next. MYH7 is a plausible alternative for a myopathy with proximal weakness. The remaining phenotypes (tumors, stroke, prostatic hyperplasia, tyrosinemia and others) look like noise. MECP2 and RET are less consistent: the negative findings for medullary thyroid carcinoma and adrenal medulla neoplasm argue against RET, and the lack of seizures argues against MECP2. The other genes carry only generic high-CADD variants with no phenotype fit.

25551.Rationale: Answered from background knowledge only; no literature search was run, and the disease ID 90674 could not be matched to a specific disorder. The phenotype list is noisy. The most specific cutaneous and developmental features (skin erosion, abnormal facial shape, infant onset, and the negatives pes cavus, hypospadias and MCP subluxation) point toward epidermal and ectodermal genes. RIPK4 (Bartsocas-Papas and popliteal pterygium spectrum) is ranked first because of skin erosion, abnormal facial features and congenital anomalies. KDSR (erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva with thrombocytopenia) and PERP (erythrokeratodermia variabilis) are next as skin-barrier genes. CENPJ (Seckel/microcephaly) and NUP88 follow as developmental genes. The remaining genes have no clear link to the phenotype. RGR, F8 and the IDs 57760 and 724107 have no variants listed and are placed last.

27134.Rationale: The phenotype set (congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, ichthyosis, amniotic constriction rings/pseudoainhum, vascular skin abnormality, infantile onset) fits loricrin keratoderma (Camisa/Vohwinkel variant), an AD disorder caused by frameshift or missense variants in LORICRIN (LOR) at the C-terminal. LORICRIN and LOR are the same gene; the rare missense variant (CADD 26.4) is listed under LOR. Other candidates have the splice,missense annotation pattern with high CADD but have no phenotypic fit with this keratinization disorder (e.g. SRY, GNAS, F2, BUB1, VPS13B, DNAH9, TUBB3, CARS2, AHCY). KLK8 and RAC1 are skin-related but are not established causes of this disorder.

37264.Rationale: This ranking comes from phenotype matching alone. I did not run a literature or database search, and I could not identify Disease ID 440437. The phenotype set mixes a CNS tumour phenotype (glioblastoma, increased intracranial pressure, seizure) with neurodevelopmental features (intellectual disability, hypotonia, developmental regression, constipation) and neuroblastoma. NSD1 best fits the overlap of hypotonia, intellectual disability, seizures, constipation and neuroblastoma, which is a recognised Sotos-spectrum tumour association. The explicit absence of tall stature and large for gestational age lowers my confidence in it. ADNP also fits ID, hypotonia, seizures, visual impairment and constipation, but the absence of delayed speech and autistic behaviour counts against it. MCPH1 (DNA damage response, neurodevelopmental, cancer-linked) and ATP2B3 (ataxia, gait disturbance) fit partially. DNMT1 is penalised because deafness and narcolepsy are absent, and RRM2B because progressive external ophthalmoplegia is absent. RPS20 is a colorectal cancer predisposition gene, and rectal neoplasm is explicitly absent. PICK1, DHH, PAPPA and HPSE have little relevance to this combination.

10349.Rationale: Infant-onset dysarthria, dyskinesia, tremor, frequent falls, tube feeding, optic atrophy and raised lactate fit a mitochondrial energy-metabolism disorder. This points to MT-ATP6 (complex V; Leigh/NARP spectrum), which has a rare, highly damaging missense variant (PP2=1.0). PDE10A is second: biallelic variants cause infantile-onset hyperkinetic movement disorder (dyskinesia, chorea, dysarthria), but it would not explain the lactate or optic atrophy. HPS1 could explain thrombocytopenia but not the neurological picture. NTRK1, RET, SAMHD1, ARSG, CA4, COL1A2 and ZNF85 do not match; the negative findings (no adrenal tumours, medullary thyroid carcinoma or hypertension) also argue against RET. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge of these genes, not from a literature search run in this session.

5171.Rationale: No literature or database lookup was done; this ranking comes from prior knowledge only. The phenotype set looks noisy, and no single gene explains it. The most consistent theme is adult-onset mitochondrial or metabolic disease with liver involvement (acute hepatitis, anemia, behavioral and pain features). On that basis POLG ranks first, since it is linked to hepatopathy and adult-onset mitochondrial disease. ETFDH (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, which can present in adults) is second. 12957.Rationale: This ranking comes from the phenotype list and my own knowledge of the genes. I did not run any literature or web searches. I could not resolve what Disease ID 35701 refers to. 38336.Rationale: Infant-onset global developmental delay, intellectual disability, microcephaly, cerebral atrophy, seizures, hypotonia, behavioral abnormality, abnormal genitalia and mild dysmorphism (low anterior hairline, broad neck) fit the HSF1-related multiple congenital anomalies-neurodevelopmental syndrome (de novo HSF1 missense variants), so HSF1 is ranked first. 14268.Rationale: Gingival fibromatosis, coarse facial features, generalized hirsutism, synophrys and cognitive impairment match Zimmermann-Laband syndrome. 26428.Rationale: The picture fits severe mevalonate kinase deficiency (mevalonic aciduria). It combines infant-onset organic aciduria, metabolic acidosis, hepatomegaly, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, micrognathia and other dysmorphism, panniculitis, feeding difficulty, temperature instability and death in infancy. The absent arthralgia, abdominal pain and raised ESR argue against the milder hyper-IgD form, and the absence of hyperammonemia and high CSF lactate argues against mitochondrial and Krebs cycle disorders. MVK carries a rare splice/missense variant with CADD 50, so it ranks first. MMMUT (methylmalonic aciduria) is a plausible organic aciduria with acidosis, but hyperammonemia is absent. The mitochondrial genes MT-ND5 and MT-TE are less likely given the normal CSF lactate. POLD1 (mandibular hypoplasia, lipodystrophy), SLC25A19 and FLVCR1 are weaker partial matches. 2641.Rationale: The core phenotype is adult-onset spastic paraplegia with hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, corticospinal tract degeneration, limb ataxia, spasms and impaired lower-limb vibration sense. Several other listed terms are noise, such as craniosynostosis, phthisis bulbi and methemoglobinemia. 40570.Rationale: Answered from recall of the literature only; I ran no searches and could not confirm what disease ID 79244 refers to. I think it is most likely a pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency entry, but that is unverified. The case combines ataxia, abnormal eye movements, gait and speech disturbance, corpus callosum hypoplasia, ventriculomegaly or hydrocephalus, growth delay and dysmorphic features (frontal bossing, hypertelorism, long philtrum). That pattern fits PDH complex deficiency, and DLAT encodes the E2 subunit. The reduced B6 and the neurological picture are also compatible. However, intellectual disability and seizures are recorded as absent, which argues against it. KCNJ11, NOA1, UTP4 and GLIS2 have only weak or indirect links to this picture. 9097.Rationale: The core phenotype cluster is abnormal leukocyte morphology (Pelger-Huet-like), brachydactyly, abnormal vertebral body form and abnormal bone ossification. 5192.Rationale: Answered from memory of the literature, without a literature search or lookup of Disease ID 79314, so the ranking is a judgement call. It has the highest CADD score, but ataxia is listed as absent, which argues against the ataxia form. 1285.Rationale: Splenomegaly, normochromic anemia and pallor are hematologic and visceral features consistent with a lysosomal storage disorder. The listed negative phenotypes (supranuclear ophthalmoplegia, oculomotor apraxia, abnormal saccades, aortic and aortic valve calcification, lipoatrophy) match the differential for Gaucher disease and its neuronopathic and cardiovascular forms, which fits GBA1. I did not run any literature search or tool lookups.

35589.Rationale: Phenotypes (infant onset, hypophosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, reduced bone mineral density, recurrent fractures, abnormal bone structure, bone cysts, short stature, dental abnormality) fit a vitamin D metabolism or signalling disorder. 5735.Rationale: Ranking is from recalled literature only; I did no searches and made no variant classification. 37047.Rationale: The phenotype is sensorineural hearing loss, cognitive impairment, short stature, a depressed nasal bridge, abnormal forehead and maxilla, ptosis, and a tented upper lip with exaggerated cupid's bow. This closely matches Keipert syndrome (nasodigitoacoustic syndrome), an X-linked disorder caused by GPC4 loss of function. The GPC4 candidate is a rare, high-CADD splice/missense variant on chrX. It lacks the facial gestalt, and dystonia and hypomyelination are not reported. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge of these disorders, not a fresh literature search.

5675.Rationale: Answered from recall of the literature only. I ran no searches and did not look up Disease ID 208447. 26534.Rationale: Infantile-onset spastic paraplegia with hyperreflexia, hypertonia, scissor gait and toe-walking is a hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) picture. Of the candidates, POLG is the only one with a documented link to HSP-like or spastic phenotypes (mitochondrial disease spectrum), and it carries a rare splice/missense variant with a very high CADD score (40). IVD (isovaleric acidemia) is a metabolic disorder that could in principle give neurological and GI signs, but it is not a typical cause of pure spastic paraplegia. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of gene-disease associations, and I did not run a literature search. The stray entry 338090 is not a gene and is excluded.

7616.Rationale: Childhood-onset progressive autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia with dysarthria, nystagmus, dysmetric saccades, limb and gait ataxia, Babinski sign, and no neuropathy or sensory loss. This fits the SCAR7 (TPP1, non-classic late-infantile CLN2 spectrum) and SCAR16 (STUB1) pictures. I did not do a literature search. This is from recall, and I am not sure which disease ID 284324 maps to. TPP1 is ranked first because SCAR7 matches a pure cerebellar ataxia with pyramidal signs, and TPP1 is the only ataxia candidate listed without a variant call. STUB1 is second because it is a strong candidate with a listed variant. Cerebellar atrophy is marked absent, which slightly weakens STUB1. ATP13A2, MFN2 and NDUFS2 are weaker ataxia or neurodegeneration candidates. The remaining genes have unrelated phenotypes. The other listed variants all carry the same generic splice/missense pattern, so I treat them as non-discriminating.

8318.Rationale: No clean single-gene syndrome matches this mixed phenotype set (limb reduction/syndactyly, sensorineural hearing loss, cloacal anomaly, plus likely noisy terms). LRP5/Wnt signaling is linked to skeletal and hand malformation and hearing loss, and the explicitly excluded bone findings (sclerosis, cortical changes, torus palatinus) match the sclerosteosis/van Buchem spectrum, which suggests a differential in that area. 13557.Rationale: Core features (spasticity, hyperreflexia, scissor and tip-toe gait) point to a hereditary spastic paraplegia, and WASHC5 (SPG8) is the only candidate gene causing classic HSP. ELOVL4 is next: biallelic variants cause spastic quadriplegia with seizures and intellectual disability, and the onset is in infancy. MED12 (FG/Lujan syndrome) could explain the hyperactivity, low-set ears and hypertonia. The remaining genes have no clear link to the phenotype. This ranking is from recalled knowledge, not a literature search, and I could not identify what Disease ID 101004 refers to (I suspect it is an HSP entry).

20503.Rationale: The positive phenotypes are optic atrophy and pallor, nystagmus, decreased nerve conduction velocity, intention tremor, gait ataxia, and intellectual disability. Together they point to a syndromic neurological disorder with optic atrophy, neuropathy and cerebellar signs. ATAD3A (Harel-Yoon syndrome) fits best, since it causes optic atrophy, axonal or demyelinating neuropathy, ataxia, tremor and cognitive impairment. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge only: I did not run a literature search, and I did not identify what disease ID 98890 refers to. POLR3B (POLR3-related hypomyelinating leukodystrophy with ataxia, tremor and nystagmus) is the next most plausible. The absent phenotypes argue against the other candidates. They exclude septo-optic dysplasia and hypopituitarism (ARNT2), Peters anomaly and anterior segment dysgenesis (FOXC1), the Townes-Brocks features of anal atresia, ear malformation and polydactyly (SALL1), and the hedgehog or cholestasis disorders (IHH, TJP2). BRAF, LSS, C1R, TNNT3, LY6E, MIR423 and H19 do not match the phenotype.

40628.Rationale: Adult-onset myopathy with rimmed vacuoles, centrally nucleated and variable-diameter fibers, mildly elevated CK, foot dorsiflexor weakness and mixed distal/proximal involvement fits a titinopathy (tibial muscular dystrophy / distal titinopathy) best. TTN has a rare splice/missense variant with very high CADD (51). FLNC (distal/myofibrillar myopathy) is the next most plausible. TP53INP2 has been reported in autophagic rimmed-vacuolar myopathy, so it ranks third. Lattice corneal dystrophy, avascular necrosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and amenorrhea look like unrelated findings. The remaining genes have no known link to a myopathy of this kind. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of the literature; I did not run a literature search in this session.

15489.Rationale: No literature or database lookup was done, so this ranking is a judgement from the phenotype list and what I recall of each gene. The phenotype set looks like a mix of unrelated terms. FGB is the clearest single match, because fibrinogen beta-chain variants cause dysfibrinogenemia and thrombophilia, which fits hypercoagulability. KAT6B and MED25 are neurodevelopmental genes that could account for seizures, memory impairment and craniofacial or dental findings such as the open bite. RIMS1 and SLC17A7 are synaptic genes that could account for seizures. RIMS1 is also linked to cone-rod dystrophy, and RHO to retinal degeneration, which fits macular degeneration. FASLG and FANCL are linked to cancer predisposition, which fits stomach cancer. EMP2 is linked to nephrotic syndrome, which is listed as absent, so it ranks low. The remaining genes have no clear match to the listed phenotypes. MED25 has no observed variant listed, which counts against it.

12927.Rationale: No gene in the list is a classic cause of a Costello/cutis-laxa-like picture (thickened skin, increased skin folds, keloids, epicanthus, infant onset, developmental delay), so this ranking is a best guess from memory and was not checked against the literature. FGFR3 is ranked first because it is the best fit for skin thickening and folds (acanthosis nigricans-type skin changes), palate and facial dysmorphism, and a RASopathy-like overlap, and its variant is rare and high-CADD. TNXB (Ehlers-Danlos-type connective tissue disorder with skin and cardiac involvement) is second. SMARCC2 explains the global developmental delay and some dysmorphism. ADAMTSL4 (epicanthus/eye findings) and NFKB2 (CADD 51 but immune phenotype absent) follow. ADAM12 is linked to preeclampsia only through association studies. APOA1, APEX1, TUBB2A and TUBB (no observed variant) are unlikely.

31134.Rationale: The picture is a childhood-onset myopathy with normal CK, raised lactate, increased muscle lipid, facial, neck and proximal weakness, restrictive lung disease and cardiomegaly. That fits a mitochondrial myopathy with lipid storage, so I ranked MT-TL1 first. MT-TL1 (tRNA-Leu UUR) variants cause mitochondrial myopathy and MELAS-spectrum disease, and the listed variant is m.3305A>T in that gene. CHCHD10 is second because it causes mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis, but it usually presents later. PPARA is third as a fatty-acid oxidation and lipid-metabolism gene. The normal CK argues against the dystrophy and limb-girdle genes DYSF, ANO5 and POMGNT1. TNNT3 (distal arthrogryposis) and COL1A2 are less likely. The remaining genes have no link to this phenotype. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of these genes. I did not search the literature or the web.

Matching features: midface retrusion, short nose, broad/prominent forehead with frontal bossing, shallow orbits with proptosis, hydronephrosis, genital abnormalities, broad ribs, profound global developmental delay, congenital heart defects, hip dislocation, sensorineural hearing loss, visual impairment, and occasional Hirschsprung disease. It would explain frontal bossing, proptosis, visual impairment from optic nerve compression, hearing loss, failure to thrive, acidosis and skeletal abnormalities, but it does not explain hydronephrosis, genital anomalies or profound developmental delay. Other candidates (USP9X, ZNF423, STT3A, SCYL1, SARDH, FOXP3, GUCY2C and the rest) do not fit the combination of midface retraction, hydronephrosis and broad ribs. SARDH is excluded because hypersarcosinemia is absent. FOXP3 is excluded because autoimmunity is absent. This ranking comes from prior knowledge of the syndromes and not from a literature search.

34754.Rationale: The pattern of abnormal dental morphology, short digits, hearing impairment, corneal opacity and visual impairment, ptosis, cleft palate, clubfoot, hypotonia and motor delay is most consistent with GJA1-related oculodentodigital dysplasia and its broader connexin 43 phenotypes. The listed negatives (absent hand, ulnar and fibular aplasia, oligodactyly, nail dysplasia) argue against the severe limb-reduction conditions that would point to WNT7A. SOX9 is a plausible second choice because of cleft palate, clubfoot and hearing loss, although the absence of micrognathia and cervical or scapular anomalies weakens it. ANK2 explains the atrial ectopy but not the rest of the picture. LAMC1 and PPP1CB are weaker, partial fits. The remaining genes have no clear link to this phenotype. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge of these genes' syndromes. I did not run a literature search or check the variants.

6302.Rationale: Infantile-onset CNS hypomyelination with nystagmus, global developmental delay/stagnation, spasticity and hyperreflexia, intention tremor, cerebral atrophy and seizures is the typical picture of a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. The candidate listed as RARS11 (ENSG00000113643) is RARS1, arginyl-tRNA synthetase. Biallelic RARS1 variants cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 9 (HLD9), which has this phenotype, so it is ranked first. This is from my own knowledge of the literature. I did no search and no variant classification. Other candidates fit only part of the picture: PLCB1 and SCN1A explain the seizures but not the hypomyelination. The rest (APOB, PIK3R1, SLC25A13, SLC27A4, JUP, CACNA2D1, MKRN3, 100049159) have no good match to this presentation.

2516.Rationale: The positive phenotypes that fit a single disease are infant-onset motor delay, difficulty walking and hyperreflexia, which suggest a motor neuron or spastic-gait disorder. BICD2 (dominant spinal muscular atrophy, lower-extremity predominant, and spastic paraplegia, with infantile onset) fits best. The other positive terms (cutis laxa, aglossia, amyelia, pulmonary hemorrhage, miscarriage) do not map to any one candidate and look like noise. The negatives (no ataxia, spastic ataxia, dystonia, lactate elevation, white matter change or status epilepticus) argue against KIF1C, PRKRA, the mitochondrial genes (MT-TK, MT-CO3) and TIMM50. The remaining genes (SHH, COL7A1, ALK, SLC30A1, VDAC2, CIB1) have no clear match. I did not check the literature or the web for this ranking, so it rests on recalled gene-phenotype associations.

8501.Rationale: Answered from recalled literature only; I ran no searches and did no variant classification. The profile combines adult-onset tachyarrhythmia (SVT, palpitations, syncope) with a sensory neuropathy and areflexia, hepatitis, acidosis and thrombocytopenia. CPOX (hereditary coproporphyria, an acute hepatic porphyria) best unifies the autonomic tachycardia, neuropathy with areflexia, hepatic involvement and acidosis, so it is ranked first. CACNA1C (arrhythmia and syncope channelopathy) is second. SLC25A3 (mitochondrial phosphate carrier deficiency, with arrhythmia and acidosis) and the cardiac genes LMNA, FLNC and CAV3 are plausible for the arrhythmia, but the cardiomyopathy and conduction-defect phenotypes are reported absent, which lowers them. GALT (galactosemia: hepatitis, acidosis) and TCF3 (leukemia and immune defects) fit only part of the picture. ELP1 is down-weighted because alacrima, hyperhidrosis and orthostatic hypotension are absent. The remaining genes have no clear link to this phenotype.

36490.Rationale: Positive phenotypes (coronary artery calcification, venous thrombosis, pancreatic abnormality such as pancreatitis, abnormal cardiovascular morphology) fit a lipid-metabolism disorder. I think ORPHA:79253 is hepatic lipase deficiency, but I did not check that ID, so this is from memory. LIPC encodes hepatic lipase, so it is the best match. PAH (PKU) and MKS1 (Joubert/Meckel) are less likely, because the neurological and ciliopathy features (severe ID, molar tooth sign, vermis hypoplasia) are explicitly absent. The remaining genes have no clear link to the phenotype. I did not search the literature or the web.

14420.Rationale: The phenotype set is noisy, so I ranked mainly on gene-phenotype fit, with no literature search done. I could not confirm what Disease ID 93605 refers to. Arrhythmia and myopathy point most strongly to ANK2 (ankyrin-B syndrome, a cardiac arrhythmia disorder with skeletal/cardiac muscle involvement), which also carries a very high CADD score of 58 at a splice/missense variant. BCKDHB and DLST are metabolic genes (amino-acid and mitochondrial energy metabolism) that loosely fit hyperargininemia, myopathy and hypolipoproteinemia. The remaining genes (immune, ciliopathy, neuronal or non-coding) have little phenotype overlap. The two non-coding genes, SAMMSON and LINC00871, are ranked last.

23142.Rationale: Infant-onset multisystem disorder with cardiac involvement (cardiomegaly, endocardial fibrosis, bradycardia), seizures, liver disease (giant cell hepatitis), glucose intolerance and mild facial dysmorphism (overfolded helix, nasal bridge changes, smooth philtrum), with intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental delay reported absent. This is ranked from memory, not from a literature search, and I could not identify Disease ID 324410 with confidence. KRAS (RASopathy: cardiac disease, dysmorphism) is the best fit for the cardiac plus dysmorphic picture. SMPD1 (infantile Niemann-Pick, which can present with giant cell hepatitis and seizures) and PIGA (seizures, liver involvement, dysmorphism) are plausible alternatives. INPPL1, LYST, SLC40A1 (neonatal liver disease) and others fit less well.

22925.Rationale: The core picture is prenatal-onset growth failure (IUGR, growth delay, failure to thrive), microtia/anotia, micrognathia and retrognathia, cleft palate, narrow mouth, delayed bone age, slender long bones, epiphyseal abnormalities, joint hyperflexibility and hypospadias. This fits Meier-Gorlin syndrome (replication licensing defect), so ORC4 ranks first. COG7 (a CDG with rib, micrognathia, contracture, failure-to-thrive features and hypovolemia) is second. RBM10 (TARP-like, but its defining features are listed as absent), RIPK4 and TP63 (orofacial cleft, skin erosions) follow. Phenotypes such as Alzheimer disease, sulfite oxidase deficiency and lattice degeneration look like noise. The remaining genes have no clear link to the phenotype. This ranking comes from recalled knowledge only; I did not run a literature search.

20359.Rationale: The positive phenotypes are adenomatous colorectal polyposis, pancreatic adenocarcinoma and an ovarian neoplasm, with onset in old age. This pattern fits a mismatch-repair (Lynch-spectrum) hereditary cancer syndrome, which includes pancreatic and ovarian tumors. MSH6 is the best match, and the observed variant is rare and has a very high CADD score of 47. MSH6-associated disease is characteristically late-onset, which also fits the elderly onset. RNF43 is second because it is linked to serrated and adenomatous polyposis and to pancreatic neoplasia. FGFR2 and RFC1 are weak because they do not explain the polyposis. The remaining genes (MYH3, GM2A, TMEM100, EDARADD, SLC19A1) are unrelated to hereditary polyposis or cancer. I ranked these from memory and did not run a literature search or database lookup. I also could not confirm what disease ID 157798 refers to.

16470.Rationale: This is a judgement from recalled knowledge only; I ran no literature or database searches. The phenotype set (antenatal intracerebral hemorrhage, abnormal dura, vascular dilatation, ventriculomegaly, cortical atrophy, abnormal fontanelle, optic nerve hypoplasia, seizures, spastic diplegia) points to a severe prenatal brain destruction or malformation, hydranencephaly-like (Fowler-like). FLVCR2, the classic Fowler gene, is not among the candidates. NDE1 is the closest fit. It causes microhydranencephaly and severe cortical malformation, and it carries a rare missense variant with CADD 47. PDHX fits next: it causes pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, which explains the raised lactate, cortical atrophy, ventriculomegaly, seizures and spasticity. FLT4 is a vascular and lymphatic gene, so it could account for the vascular dilatation. CTNNB1 and GJA1 are plausible neurodevelopmental and ocular candidates. Many other candidates match the negative phenotypes (SLC39A8 for hypomanganesemia, CASK for cerebellar hypoplasia, ODAD2/ARMC4 for immotile cilia, POU1F1 for hypopituitarism, GATA6, IHH and EYA1 for other syndromes), so they are ranked low. The remaining genes are non-specific.

37973.Rationale: Based on recall of the literature; I did not run a literature search. The phenotype is an ectodermal dysplasia pattern: sparse scalp and pubic hair, nail dysplasia and fragile nails, generalized hyperpigmentation, skin ulcers and actinic keratosis. It also has ocular findings (photophobia, cataract, strabismus). GJB6 (connexin 30) is the best fit because its missense variants cause Clouston syndrome (hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia), with hypotrichosis, nail dystrophy and skin hyperpigmentation. The absence of sensorineural hearing loss also fits, since Clouston syndrome does not usually include deafness. GJB6 has a rare missense variant with CADD 32. FOXN1 is second because variants in it cause nail dystrophy and alopecia. The other candidates (SARS1 and CLCN4 for cognitive impairment, CYP2U1 for spastic paraplegia, TSHB for thyroid disease, and the rest) fit the skin, hair and nail picture poorly. Genes with no observed variant (RGPD2, PRPS1) are ranked last.

21304.Rationale: Assessed from recall of the literature only; no search was run. The phenotype set is a multiple congenital anomaly syndrome with polydactyly and syndactyly, ocular coloboma, corpus callosum hypoplasia, ventriculomegaly, hypertelorism, intestinal malrotation, seizures and hypopigmented skin patches. This fits a hedgehog-pathway / midline-patterning disorder. SMO (Smoothened) is linked to Curry-Hall-type polydactyly and malformation syndrome, so it is ranked first. It is the only candidate listed without an observed variant, which may mean it is the intended disease gene, though that is a guess. PIGN (multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome 1) is a strong second. It matches on corpus callosum hypoplasia, seizures, polydactyly, syndactyly and malformations, and it carries a high-CADD splice/missense variant (CADD 52). IRX3 is a minor developmental-patterning candidate. The remaining genes have no convincing link to this phenotype and are ranked low.

21075.Rationale: No literature or database lookup was done; this ranking is a judgement from the phenotype list and my background knowledge. The negatives (hemolytic anemia, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmunity, myopathy, aminoaciduria, spinocerebellar degeneration) argue against the ALPS-like genes (CASP10, FASLG, RASGRP1, PRKCD) and against GCLC deficiency. The infantile-onset neurological picture (microcephaly, intellectual disability, seizures, memory impairment, subarachnoid hemorrhage) fits SLC19A3 (thiamine transporter dysfunction) and mitochondrial tRNA disease (MT-TK, MERRF-like) best. PHF8 (X-linked intellectual disability) is also plausible. TGFB1 fits the pain, myalgia, fatigue, hyperalgesia and joint abnormality. HBB and ABCB6 fit the red-cell findings (reticulocytosis, raised MCV) but not the neurological ones. The remaining genes have no clear link to the phenotypes.

39784.Rationale: Phenotype is an infantile-onset multisystem mitochondrial-type picture: cardiomyopathy, skeletal muscle atrophy, abnormal CK, reduced tendon reflexes, microcephaly, seizures, global developmental delay, ataxia, ventriculomegaly, visual impairment, ptosis and aminoaciduria. SCO2 (COX assembly; fatal infantile cardioencephalomyopathy) best fits the cardiomyopathy, muscle and CNS features. SUCLA2 (encephalomyopathic mtDNA depletion with methylmalonic aciduria) is next, matching microcephaly, seizures, hypotonia/atrophy and aminoaciduria. GPAA1 (GPI-anchor deficiency) fits seizures, delay, cerebellar involvement and the elevated alkaline phosphatase. SDHB and FXN are less likely: FXN is mainly later-onset ataxia, and SDHB is not a typical infantile encephalopathy gene. TTN, TPM2 and DCTN1 are only partial fits for the muscle or cardiac findings. NSDHL (X-linked, CHILD syndrome) and the remaining genes have little phenotypic support. This ranking is based on prior knowledge, not a literature search.

33733.Rationale: Answered from recalled literature only, with no database or web lookup. The core picture is infant-onset encephalopathy with global developmental delay, spasticity, progressive cerebral atrophy, abnormal myelination and microcephaly. This best matches INPP4A-related autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder, which has been reported with severe delay, spasticity, microcephaly and cerebral atrophy. The INPP4A variant is also a high-CADD rare splice/missense. HUWE1 (X-linked syndromic intellectual disability with microcephaly) is next, followed by SYNJ1 (early-onset epileptic encephalopathy), DDHD2 (complex spastic paraplegia, though spastic paraplegia is listed as absent) and CHD7 (CHARGE-like features, short stature and pituitary involvement, but poor fit for the neurodegeneration). The remaining genes are not linked to this neurological phenotype, and the odd findings (Schmorl's node, gastric eosinophilic infiltration, otitis externa) look like noise.

27610.Rationale: Liver dysfunction with ascites and abnormal liver morphology, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, myositis and failure to thrive best fit glycogen branching enzyme deficiency (GSD IV, GBE1), which causes progressive hepatic disease with cirrhosis and ascites, cardiomyopathy and muscle involvement. GBE1 also carries a very high CADD variant (40). HADHA (trifunctional protein/LCHAD deficiency) is a second option, since it causes liver dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, myopathy and failure to thrive. SPEG (cardiomyopathy and myopathy) and TMEM43 (cardiomyopathy) are weaker matches. PPARG (lipodystrophy, insulin resistance) conflicts with the absent lipoatrophy and diabetes. SARDH (sarcosinemia) conflicts with the absent hypersarcosinemia. The remaining genes do not match the phenotype. This ranking comes from my own recall of the literature; I did not run a literature search or check the disease ID against a database.

36785.Rationale: Assessed from recalled literature only; no search was run. The adult-onset picture is cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, tremor, hyperreflexia, memory impairment, cerebellar atrophy and hypermetric saccades. This best matches the neurodegenerative spectrum of C9orf72 repeat-expansion disease, which includes cerebellar ataxia, cognitive decline and upper motor neuron signs. The renal, lung, infertility and pretragal findings do not point to any candidate and look like noise. Other candidates with some neurological or multisystem relevance (TMEM43, EMD, AP1S1, DHCR24, SLC25A3, RAB4A) are ranked lower, and the remaining genes are unlikely.
